messages.subject_clean: Manually convert from unstandardized to standardized coefficients
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Maybe this is not so much a lavaan question as a latent modeling question in general.

Let's say that I have a simple 2-factor latent model like this:

model <- '
A =~ A1 + A2 + A3
A ~~ A
B =~ B1 + B2 + B3
B ~~ B
A ~~ B
'
fit <- cfa(model = model, data = data)
summary(fit)

Without the std = TRUE argument, summary will only display unstandardized coefficients.

Due to some very complicated reasons, I need to calculate the standardized coefficients manually and not through the usage of std = T argument.

I am interested in calculating the standardized coefficient A ~~ B and A =~ A2, given their unstandardized values printed by the usage of summary. What would be the formula to achieve this?

christia...@hhl.de 在 2023年1月29日 星期日晚上7:34:00 [UTC+8] 的信中寫道：

> In principle, you can bootstrap all conceivable coefficients. The procedure is basically as follows:
>
> (1) Write a function that extracts the desired coefficients. Execute bootstrapLavaan.
> (2) Write a function that computes the CI. Pass the object created with bootstrapLavaan.
> (3) Print the results.
>
> Here's an example:
>
> library(lavaan)
>
> pop.model <- "
> ER =~ 1.0 * socb13 + 1.0 * socb14 + 1.0* socb15 + 1.0 * socb16
> WDR =~ 1.0 * socb24 + 1.0 * socb25 + 1.0 * socb26
> DAD =~ 1.0 * fatherinvo01 + 1.0 * fatherinvo02 + 1.0 * fatherinvo03 + 1.0 * fatherinvo04 + 1.0 * fatherinvo05
> MOM =~ 1.0 * motherinvo01 + 1.0 * motherinvo02 + 1.0 * motherinvo03 + 1.0 * motherinvo04 + 1.0 * motherinvo05
>
> ER ~ 0.3 * DAD + 0.4 * MOM
> WDR ~ 0.5 * ER + 0.2 * DAD+ 0.4 * MOM
> "
>
> dta <- simulateData(pop.model, sample.nobs = 2000)
>
> model<-
> 'ER=~socb13+socb14+socb15+socb16
> WDR=~socb24+socb25+socb26
> DAD=~fatherinvo01+fatherinvo02+fatherinvo03+fatherinvo04+fatherinvo05
> MOM=~motherinvo01+motherinvo02+motherinvo03+motherinvo04+motherinvo05
>
> ER~a*DAD+b*MOM
> WDR~c*ER+d*DAD+e*MOM
>
> med1 := a*c
> med2 := b*c
> tot_X1Y := a*c+d
> tot_X2Y := b*c+e'
>
> result <- sem(model, dta)
>
>
> # Std. estimates
> get.std <- function(obj) {
>   sl <- standardizedsolution(obj)
>   res <- sl[, "est.std"]
>   names(res) <- paste0(sl[, "lhs"], sl[, "op"], sl[, "rhs"])
>   res
> }
>
> # 95% perc CI
> get.ci <http://get.ci> <- function(obj) {
>   alpha <- c(0.025, 0.975)
>   ci <- sapply(colnames(obj), function(column, obj, alpha) {
>     c(
>       ci.lower = as.numeric(quantile(obj[, column], alpha[1], type = 6)),
>       ci.upper = as.numeric(quantile(obj[, column], alpha[2], type = 6))
>     )
>   }, obj, alpha)
>   t(ci)
> }
>
>
> boot <- bootstrapLavaan(result, R = 100, FUN = get.std, verbose = TRUE)
> ci   <- get.ci <http://get.ci>(boot)
>
> cbind(
>   standardizedsolution(result)[, c("lhs", "op", "rhs", "est.std")],
>   ci
> )
>
> An easy-to-use and more general solution can be found here: https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/0RSsh4M6zQg/m/03uaQYpyAQAJ
>
> Best
>
> Christian

messages.subject: Re: se = "bootstrap" and fixed.x
messages.body_plain:
This is a follow-up to a question I posted myself a while ago.

I did some experiments and it seems that, when fixed.x = TRUE and se = "bootstrap", the default for a path model, the variances and covariances of x-variables are fixed to their sample values, as expected when they are treated as fixed.

However, how are the y-variables sampled? In multiple regression, if the predictors are treated as fixed, bootstrapping can be done on the residuals. I am not sure whether this is what lavaan does when se = "bootstrap" and fixed.x are used together.

In this setting, for a path model with only observed variables, is the bootstrapping conducted residual bootstrapping, using the residuals of the y-variables as in multiple regression?

If not, does it mean that the y-variables, instead of their residuals, are used in bootstrapping? This sounds strange because it is analogous to doing bootstrapping only on the outcome variable in multiple regression.

-- Shu Fai

May I ask a quick question about lavaan's bootstrapping se/ci?

- When fixed.x = TRUE, how are the bootstrap samples drawn?

In bootstrapping in multiple regression, if predictors are treated as fixed, then residual bootstrapping will be used. Is this how lavaan does bootstrapping when fixed.x = TRUE (the default of lavaan), fixing the values of x variables across bootstrap samples?

I checked the "se" section of the help page of lavOptions but it does not mention whether fixed.x will be taken into account.

-- Shu Fai

messages.subject: How to use Spearman's correlation in lavaan?
messages.subject_clean: How to use Spearman's correlation in lavaan?
messages.body_plain:
I would appreciate your comments on the following aspect of a replication project:

The aim is to conduct a unidimensional factor analysis. The relevant variables are the rank-order of a set of 8 objects and, long story short, I would fit a CFA with these rank-order variables. (I recognize there is contention on running factor analysis with rank-order and ipsative data, and a models have been proposed for that e.g. https://doi.org/10.1177/004912418000900206 and https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02294861 etc. but this goes way beyond the aims of the project.)
The available information is just the data set with the rank-ordering where each object if ranked from 1st to 8th is carried out by respondents.

Two analyses are to be conductd in two ways:
(1) Using the complete ranking of the variables (from 1st to 8th);
(2) Using a partial/tied ranking, variables are recoded as binaries where 1=the object is in the top 4 objects (i.e., ranked 1st-4th), 0=else.

Given this scenario, I wonder whether there is a way to use Spearman's rank correlation instead of, say, polychoric correlation in lavaan.

I noticed that Polychoric correlation and Spearman's correlation return very similar results for the complete rankings however there are differences for the dichotomous variables. The Spearman's correlation for the binary variables is very similar to the results for complete ranking; when polychoric correlation is used the correlations for the binary variables are considerably stronger than Spearman's (for instance, a -0.22 correlation becomes -0.34) and I am concerned on how this could affect the results.

I hope my question is not too convoluted!

NB: lavaan support using a covariance matrix as input but it is unclear to me whether the procedure applies to correlation matrix https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/tutorial.pdf

messages.subject: Re: Checking CLPM syntax for possible design errors
messages.subject_clean: Checking CLPM syntax for possible design errors
messages.body_plain:
Dear Terrence,

I am facing the same problem detailed below.

- One of them ('endo2') is a binary observed variable

This will be a problem because results will differ across (arbitrary) identification constraints.  Try fitting an AR model just to that variable (on 5 occasions), once withparameterization="delta" and once with parameterization="theta".  Compare the standardized solutions and notice they are not the same.  If you have df>0 (e.g., because the AR paths are equal), you will also have different fit stats, proving the models are not equivalent.  The reason is that the latent-response scales are not linked across time, and there is no way to do so with only 1 threshold per item that you can constrain to equality over time.  To obtain a solution, all you can do is pretend that it is reasonable to assume either marginal or residual variances (delta or theta) are equal over time, neither of which is likely to be true.  Linking scales over time would require 2 thresholds, as discussed in this article about growth-curve models.

I got - as expected - different results by applying the different parameterizations when I want to estimate an AR model for the binary variable over time. I am fixing the only threshold at each occasion to zero and constraining the underlying variance to one - that should be coherent with the "delta" parameterization, to ensure the identification of the auxiliary model linking the observed binary to the underlying variables. The results are very different and the theta parameterization seems to provide a better fit.

When I try to fit the AR model for a categorical variable - with four categories - still I encounter these differences in the fit.

I know that is expected but I am struggling a bit to understand (theoretically) - in this specific case - what determines that difference using the two parameterization and how to select one parameterization over the other a priori.

Thanks a lot!
Silvia

messages.body_plain:
I am interested in calculating the standardized coefficient A ~~ B and A =~ A2, given their unstandardized values printed by the usage of summary. What would be the formula to achieve this?

For standardize a covariance:
Cor(x,y) = Cov(x,y) / sqrt( var(x) * var(y) )

To standardize a slope:
Beta*(y ~ x) = Beta(y ~ x) * sd(x) / sd(y)

You can find the model-implied variances on the diagonal of lavInspect(fit, "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>"), and SDs are their square-roots.

lavaan will analyze whatever sample.cov= argument you provide.  The SEs and tests will not be trustworthy unless your residual variances are fixed to ensure the total variance = 1 (by definition).  In practice, you could label all the parameters, then constrain residual variances to == 1 minus the explained variance (which can be difficult to calculate in complex models).

messages.subject: Estimator for categorical variables on Multigroup CFA
messages.subject_clean: Estimator for categorical variables on Multigroup CFA
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I'm running quite a challenging Multigroup CFA with 9 samples of very different N (900, 500, 1200, 450, 500, 600, 230, 230 and 500) with categorical variables (4-point Likert scale) and a seven-factor model (each factor loaded by 5-6 items). Thus the general sample is big, and the model is complicated. This is a challenge as it makes it difficult to obtain the good fit indices and obtain measurment invariance. Traditional criteria are too restrictive and less restrictive ones were postulated to be used (like delta CFI of less than.020 instead of.010 for the difference between configural and metric models). Chi square od bot decisive because of the sample size.

Therefore I decided to use WLSM od WLSMV, with the last one being preferable.  Unfortunately, the R lavaan output gives robust CFI, TLI and RMSEA only in the case of WLSM (I mean the lines with robust fit indices, not the column; those reported in the column are frequently much worse than standard fit indices or the other robust ones, which makes it impossible to obtain a good fit with such a complicated model). WLSMV resulted in very good standard fit indices, weak robust indices and strange result in terms of a comparison between configural and metric models, as the metric model had better fit than the configural.

At the same time, the robust CFI, TLI and RMSEA presented only with the use of WLSM are good, and that relates also to configural and metric models.

I have three questions referring to this situation.
1) Is it ok to use WLSM and its robust statistics in such situation? Is it possible that in some cases WLSM is a better choice?
2) in the case of MLM and MLMV point robust fit indices are the same and there is a possibility to correct the RMSEA CIs and use robust fit indices with MLMV. Is this also a case with WLSMV? There is a manuscript from 2018 about it, maybe anything changed since that time?
3) why WLSMV gave better fit for the metric model than for the configural one?

I will be thankful for any help.

Best wishes,
Maria

Rena,
I am not sure that I understand what you mean by "first".  I wondered whether you could incorporate the moderation part of your model by simultaneously fitting the model to the three groups as a 3-group analysis.  It is not obvious why that would lead to convergence problems unless you fit the model with all the cross-group constraints and these were not consistent with the data generating process.  If you still get convergence problems without cross-group constraints, then I would try fitting each group one at a time to troubleshoot where the convergence problems originate from.  Of course, if you are fallible like me, it is also worth checking for syntax errors in the 3-group model that you fit.  You may have overlooked something.

messages.subject: Re: se = "bootstrap" and fixed.x
messages.body_plain:
On 2/2/23 07:19, Shu Fai Cheung (張樹輝) wrote:
> However, how are the y-variables sampled? In multiple regression, if the
> predictors are treated as fixed, bootstrapping can be done on the
> residuals. I am not sure whether this is what lavaan does when se =
> "bootstrap" and fixed.x are used together.

Nothing special. It just samples the rows of the original sample as
usual, and for each fit, we use fixed.x = TRUE.

In that sense, using fixed.x = TRUE or fixed.x = FALSE has little impact
on the bootstrap standard errors of the regression coefficients. That
also seems true for the analytic standard errors. Consider these three
examples:

fit1 <- sem(model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, fixed.x = FALSE)
parameterEstimates(fit1) |> subset(op == "~")

fit2 <- sem(model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, fixed.x = TRUE)
parameterEstimates(fit2) |> subset(op == "~")

fit3 <- sem(model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, conditional.x = TRUE)
parameterEstimates(fit3) |> subset(op == "~")

which results three times in

   lhs op rhs   est    se     z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
1  x9  ~  x1 0.254 0.051 4.998  0.000    0.155    0.354
2  x9  ~  x2 0.049 0.048 1.025  0.305   -0.045    0.144
3  x9  ~  x3 0.160 0.053 3.004  0.003    0.056    0.265

Having said this, at the beginning of the file lav_bootstrap.R, I wrote
(circa 2012):

"Question: if fixed.x=TRUE, should we not keep X fixed, and bootstrap Y
  only, conditional on X??"

So I wondered about this too...

Yves.

messages.subject_clean: Estimator for categorical variables on Multigroup CFA
messages.body_plain:
On 2/3/23 23:18, Maria Cyniak-Cieciura wrote:
> I have three questions referring to this situation.
> 1) Is it ok to use WLSM and its robust statistics in such situation?

I am afraid not. But the WLSMV 'scaled' versions are not ok either. See

Savalei, V. (2021) Improving Fit Indices In SEM with categorical data.
Multivariate Behavioral Research, 56(3), 390-407.

> 2) in the case of MLM and MLMV point robust fit indices are the same and
> there is a possibility to correct the RMSEA CIs and use robust fit
> indices with MLMV. Is this also a case with WLSMV?

In the last version of lavaan (0.6-13), we implemented the Savalei
(2021) method for handling categorical data. This seems to be the best
method we have for the moment. But it is only available for models
without covariates or any other continuous variables. This should result
in 'Robust' values for CFI and RMSEA.

> 3) why WLSMV gave better fit for the metric model than for the
> configural one?

That is (unfortunately) an artifact of the (non-robust) WLSMV fit
measures. They are way too optimistic...

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks a lot for your explanation! So it seems that, for se = "boot", fixed.x = TRUE or FALSE does not matter.

However, would it be an issue when users use bootstrapLavaan() directly, and do something that involves statistics related to the x-variables? This is an illustration:

library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-13
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.

set.seed(89415)
n <- 100
x1 <- rnorm(n)
x2 <- rnorm(n)
m <- .7 * x1 + sqrt(1 - .7^2) * rnorm(n)
y <- .4 * m + .3 * x1 + sqrt(1 - .4^2 - .3^2) * rnorm(n)
dat <- data.frame(x1, x2, m, y)
dat <- data.frame(scale(dat, scale = FALSE))
head(dat)
#>           x1          x2           m           y
#> 1  0.1700550  1.62868780  1.01709713  0.72425196
#> 2  0.3696030 -0.05364172  0.59204034  3.25913778
#> 3  1.1762182  0.39409649  2.09291261  0.83745128
#> 4 -0.6597227 -1.48842864  0.07530407 -0.08926538
#> 5  0.6730548 -0.21396188  1.19325476  2.05601816
#> 6 -2.0949939 -0.84634186 -1.65592095 -1.71790067

mod <-
"
m ~ x1 + x2
y ~ m + x1 + x2
"

fit_fixed.x <- sem(model = mod, data = dat, fixed.x = TRUE)

get_x <- function(fit) {
    est_p <- c(1:3, 8:10)
    parameterEstimates(fit)[est_p, "est"]
  }
est_p <- c(1:3, 8:10)
est_names <- apply(parameterEstimates(fit_fixed.x)[, 1:3], 1,
                   paste0, collapse = "")[est_p]
boot_fixed.x <- bootstrapLavaan(fit_fixed.x, R = 100,
                          FUN = get_x,
                          iseed = 598327)
colnames(boot_fixed.x) <- est_names
# Variances and covariances of x1 and x2 in each bootstrap replication
head(boot_fixed.x, 3)
#>           m~x1        m~x2       y~m    x1~~x1     x1~~x2   x2~~x2
#> [1,] 0.6751240 -0.10585125 0.4970804 0.9122536 0.08525006 1.056212
#> [2,] 0.5492521  0.01722119 0.3113083 0.9122536 0.08525006 1.056212
#> [3,] 0.7429272 -0.19092327 0.1215204 0.9122536 0.08525006 1.056212
# Variances and covariances of x1 and x2 in original results
parameterEstimates(fit_fixed.x)[est_p, "est"]
#> [1]  0.62553604 -0.04867653  0.28130799  0.91225364  0.08525006  1.05621202

fit_random.x <- sem(model = mod, data = dat, fixed.x = FALSE)
boot_random.x <- bootstrapLavaan(fit_random.x, R = 100,
                          FUN = get_x,
                          iseed = 598327)
colnames(boot_random.x) <- est_names
# Variances and covariances of x1 and x2 in each bootstrap replication
head(boot_random.x, 3)
#>           m~x1        m~x2       y~m    x1~~x1     x1~~x2   x2~~x2
#> [1,] 0.6751240 -0.10585124 0.4970804 0.8123582 0.17905381 1.005422
#> [2,] 0.5492521  0.01722119 0.3113083 0.8331755 0.08982125 1.132758
#> [3,] 0.7429272 -0.19092328 0.1215204 0.7599992 0.02083548 1.075500

As you explained, the estimates of the free parameters (the three regression coefficients) are the same in each bootstrap sample, whether fixed.x is TRUE or FALSE.

However, the variances and covariances of the x-variables are indeed (correctly) fixed in each bootstrap sample when fixed.x = TRUE.

On the one hand, this is what we expect when we set fixed.x to TRUE.

On the other hand, with seed identical, comparing the corresponding bootstrap samples with fixed.x = TRUE (in boot_fixed.x) and fixed.x = FALSE (in boot_random.x), it sounds strange to have the same parameter estimates for the free parameters given that the variances and covariances of the x-variables are different.

Nevertheless, I do not yet have an idea whether and when things will go wrong. Maybe it is not an issue in common scenarios.

-- Shu Fai

messages.subject: Re: CFA warning message
messages.body_plain:
Gouvide,
You can think of the broader conceptual issue with residual covariances in this way:  You are fitting a model to a covariance matrix.  If you free all the residual covariances between the variables, this is sufficient to trivially reproduce their covariance matrix and any additional free parameters are redundant.  As a general rule, the more residual covariances you free, the less work there is for the rest of your model parameters to do.

So, it is actually progress that you now have negative variances.  This probably indicates that you now have enough constraints in your model to make it testable.  Quite possibly what this indicates is that your observed covariance matrix cannot be reproduced by your model structure.  Some variables may covary more than the model predicts and some parameters may therefore be estimated in a biased manner in an attempt to accommodate that.

You have two variables with negative disturbance variances, suggesting that the model is trying to predict more variance in those variables than they have.  One possibility is that,  because they are both means, your mean variables covary with one another more than they covary with other measures that are not means.  You could conceptualize that as shared method variance.  If you have enough observed variables, you can model that using multi-trait, multi-method models.  Otherwise, you might try simply removing the mean indicator for F1 from the model.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.subject_clean: CFA models parameters and Satorra-Bentler adjustment
messages.body_plain:
Noelline,
It is important to distinguish model parameters (like factor loadings, effect coefficients and variances) from fit indices (like CFA, TLA and RMSEA).  (There is a further distinction that can be made between indices with no known distribution (like CFA and TLS) and fit statistics with known distributions, like RMSEA) but this distinction is not as fundamental or generally recognized.)

There are different perspectives in the literature on how best to evaluate fit.  However, one common view is that it is not a good idea to rely on any one fit index (or statistic) to tell the whole story.  It is important to evaluate parameter estimates, model residuals, and a profile of summary statistics in making judgments about model fit. You can find a detailed discussion of assessing model fit in Rex Kline's SEM text.

I am not sure whether your second question refers to parameters or fit indices.  See the "estimator" section of the lavOptions help file for a description of what is and is not affected by the adjustment.  The most direct way to confirm that you have successfully requested the adjustment might be to directly compare the model chi-square values.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus

Dear Gouvide,

I do not have a solution but I am thinking about what else you can explore.

I tried to recover the covariance matrix from the eigenvalues and vectors, and then examine the correlations. Some of them are .80 or even .90. I don't know what the columns represent but maybe you can check whether some indicators are so strongly correlated that you may consider using only one of them.

You can also try fitting a CFA model with only F1 (Rainfall, Min_Relative.Humidity, Max_Relative.Humidity) because it is Min_Relative.Humidity that has a negative error variance:

cfaMod2_F1 <- "F1 =~ Rainfall + Min_Relative.Humidity + Max_Relative.Humidity"

The 3-indicator-1-factor model is a saturated model. We usually don't fit this model. However, I came across cases in which the error variance of an indicator can be negative in this saturated model, regardless of sample size. Maybe your case has a similar problem. If yes, then the solution may be different, although I do not yet know what the solution is, other than removing one of the indicators.

-- Shu Fai

messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan usera,

I am looking for advice regarding lagged influence of binary factor on outcome variable at specific time.

For example, I want to know if presence / absense of an infection in last 2 years has any impact on the outcome variable (FEV1 in my case).
I have measurements of the outcome variable in year 1-4 (x1,x2,x3,x4) and data on infection during these years (f1,f2,f3,f4).
What I'm trying to fit is
x2 as a function of f1
x3 as function of f1 and f2
x4 as a function of f2 and f3
I don't fit x1 as I don't have data on infection before the study.

Model synthax is here:
model ='intercept =~ 1*x1 + 1*x2 + 1*x3 + 1*x4
slope =~ 1*x1 + 2*x2 + 3*x3 + 4*x4
x2 ~ f1
x3 ~ f1 +f2
x4 ~ f2 + f3
'
Unfortunately, I receive warnings:

Warning messages:
1: In lav_samplestats_icov(COV = cov[[g]], ridge = 1e-05, x.idx = x.idx[[g]],  :
  lavaan WARNING: sample covariance matrix is not positive-definite
2: In lavaan::lavaan(model = model, data = for_lavaan, model.type = "growth",  :
  lavaan WARNING:
    Model estimation FAILED! Returning starting values.

Any inputs are greatly appreciated, thanks

Sincerely,
Dmitrii

messages.body_plain:
Hi Gouvidé

Your negative variance result happens for a number of reasons.

One reason is randomness. It is possible to set a negative value to a small positive value if the standard error range crosses zero into positive territory and if there is evidence from previous studies that the true value is positive.

In your case

Variances:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all

.Min_Rltv.Hmdty   -0.046    0.012   -3.811    0.000   -0.046   -0.046
the value for this variable is clearly much larger than the standard error (see the z value) so you should not force it to become .005

So this speaks to a serious mis-specification of your model.

I suspect this variable is highly correlated with .Max_Rltv.Hmdty  (I bet these are statistically and logically linearly dependent). In that case I would delete one of these two variables (preferably the one with the negative error value).

 See

Chen, F., Bollen, K. A., Paxton, P., Curran, P. J., & Kirby, J. B. (2001). Improper solutions in structural equation models: Causes, consequences, and strategies. Sociological Methods & Research, 29(4), 468-508. https://doi.org/10.1177/0049124101029004003

> Hi Gouvidé
>
> Your negative variance result happens for a number of reasons.
>
> One reason is randomness. It is possible to set a negative value to a small positive value if the standard error range crosses zero into positive territory and if there is evidence from previous studies that the true value is positive.
>
> In your case
>

>

>
> So this speaks to a serious mis-specification of your model.
>

> > > > > Gouvide,
> > > > > You can think of the broader conceptual issue with residual covariances in this way:  You are fitting a model to a covariance matrix.  If you free all the residual covariances between the variables, this is sufficient to trivially reproduce their covariance matrix and any additional free parameters are redundant.  As a general rule, the more residual covariances you free, the less work there is for the rest of your model parameters to do.
> > > > >
> > > > > So, it is actually progress that you now have negative variances.  This probably indicates that you now have enough constraints in your model to make it testable.  Quite possibly what this indicates is that your observed covariance matrix cannot be reproduced by your model structure.  Some variables may covary more than the model predicts and some parameters may therefore be estimated in a biased manner in an attempt to accommodate that.
> > > > >
> > > > > You have two variables with negative disturbance variances, suggesting that the model is trying to predict more variance in those variables than they have.  One possibility is that,  because they are both means, your mean variables covary with one another more than they covary with other measures that are not means.  You could conceptualize that as shared method variance.  If you have enough observed variables, you can model that using multi-trait, multi-method models.  Otherwise, you might try simply removing the mean indicator for F1 from the model.

> what if the residuals of M are correlated with residuals of M?
>
> Do you mean M with Y?
>
> Think for example that we have heteroskedasticity.
>
> That's not heteroskedasticity.
>
> If you want to specify a nonzero parameter using simsem matrices, it has to be specified as freely estimated in the free= matrix; otherwise, any nonzero popParam= value will be ignored.  Obviously, you can't estimate both M~~Y and Y~M, so you could only pass this model to sim(..., generate=). > As in the good ‘ol LISREL days, is it possible to input a correlation
> matrix and then a standard deviation matrix into lavaan, and have it
> compute the covariance matrix from those two matrices?

Not directly in the sem/lavaan function. But lavaan provides the
convenience function getCov() (see ?getCov) that will construct the
covariance matrix from a correlation matrix and a vector of standard
deviations.

Yves.

messages.subject_clean: Unacceptable decreasing fit in multigroup comparison
messages.body_plain:
Dear Lavaan Community,
I was fitting a model, which is quite good in its fit indices and measurement blocks without any necessary modifications. The multigroup comparison (with SAM) worked as well. But I still have to test for  measurement invariance in order to proceeed with the coefficients comparison. (I am using the multigroup to test the categorical moderator).

 The time I was computing the multigroup CFA, my fit measures became worse (unacceptable) and I cannot find any reason for it.

>From the "normal" CFA without the grouping to the multigroup comparison:
 cfi :  0.943 --> 0.855
rmsea :0.055 --> 0.094
 srmr -->   0.047 -->0.080

My Syntax is pretty much the same for the grouping and non-grouping:

fit.mg_configurial <- cfa(messmodell103, data = myData3, estimator = "MLR",missing = "FIML",group = 'zufall',
              std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

fit.mg <http://fit.mg> <- cfa(messmodell103, data = myData3, estimator = "MLR",missing = "FIML",
              std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

I did attach the output of my multigroup comparison with the bad fit indices.

I have to admit, that my sample is really really small given the high number of variables and a comparison between 4 groups (n= 301 with 25 missings). I still struggle if I can continue with the model due to that fact and was wondering if this might be the case for the bad fit.

I was inspecting all groups, loadings and more and everything looks fine. All indicators are significantly loading on their respective variables with on exception in one group, but deleting the entire constructs is not changing the fit.

I am very grateful about any idea what to further inspect as the source.

Best regards,
Madita

El miércoles, 20 de julio de 2022 a las 8:37:06 UTC-5, christia...@hhl.de escribió:
> Hi Frank,
>
> Let's start with a simple 3 group model and simulate some data:
>
> library(lavaan)
>
>
>
> pop.model <- "f =~ 1.0 * x1 + 0.9 * x2 + 0.9 * x3"
>
>
>
> n = 10000
>
> set.seed(1)
>
> data <- rbind(
>
>   simulateData(paste(pop.model, "f ~ 1.0 * 1", sep = "\n"), sample.nobs = n),
>
>   simulateData(paste(pop.model, "f ~ 2.0 * 1", sep = "\n"), sample.nobs = n),
>
>   simulateData(paste(pop.model, "f ~ 2.4 * 1", sep = "\n"), sample.nobs = n)
>
> )
>
> data$g <- rep(1 : 3, each = n)
>
> The mean of the lv in the first group is 1.0, the mean of the lv in the second group is 2.0, and the mean of the lv in the third group is 2.4. We specify the model and set an arbitrary mean value for the lv in any group. This group is now the "reference group". We specify the mean differences using parameters:
>
> model <- "
>
> f =~ x1 + x2 + x3
>
> f ~ c(m1, m2, m3)
>
> m1 == 10
>
> diff.g2.g1 := m2 - m1
>
> diff.g3.g1 := m3 - m1
>
> diff.g3.g2 := m3 - m2
>
> "
>
>
>
> In our case, the mean value of the lv in the first group is 10. The first group is thus the "reference group". We fit the model and obtain the correct mean differences:
>
> fit <- cfa(model, data, group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts"), meanstructure = TRUE, group = "g")
>
> pe  <- parameterestimates(fit)
>
> pe[pe$op == ":=",]
>
> Since we can also set the mean of the "reference group" to zero (which is common), two out of three mean differences are provided "free of charge":
>
> model <- "
>
> f =~ x1 + x2 + x3
>
> f ~ c(m1, m2, m3) * 1
>
> m1 == 0
>
> diff.g2.g1 := m2 - m1
>
> diff.g3.g1 := m3 - m1
>
> diff.g3.g2 := m3 - m2
>
> "
>
>
>
> fit <- cfa(model, data, group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts"), meanstructure = TRUE, group = "g")
>
> pe  <- parameterestimates(fit)
>
> pe[pe$op == "~1" & pe$lhs == "f",]
>
> pe[pe$op == ":=",]
>
> One could come up with the idea to completely abandon the definition of a "reference group" by applying effect coding:
>
> model <- "
>
> f =~ x1 + x2 + x3
>
> f ~ c(m1, m2, m3) * 1
>
> diff.g2.g1 := m2 - m1
>
> diff.g3.g1 := m3 - m1
>
> diff.g3.g2 := m3 - m2
>
> "
>
> fit <- cfa(model, data, effect.coding = TRUE, group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts"), meanstructure = TRUE, group = "g")
>
> pe  <- parameterestimates(fit)
>
> pe[pe$op == ":=",]
>
> Note: The results are obviously biased (which was to be expected)!
>
> HTH
>
> Christian

messages.subject: Higher-Order CR with compRelSEM in semTools
messages.subject_clean: Higher-Order CR with compRelSEM in semTools
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
McDonald (1999) defined two reliability measures for higher-order factors: omega-total (𝜔T) and omega-hierarchical (𝜔h). From my understanding both are interesting when evaulating the reliability of a higher-order model (e.g., Cheung et al., 2023).

The compRelSEM package of the semTools package outputs a general statistic when a higher factor is defined. Does this general statistic refer to the 𝜔T or 𝜔h?
Wouldn't it be useful to have an option to see them both?

Best,
Lucas

Dear Yves,
Thank you very very much for your reply. It made it all pretty clear for me.

One more question about cfa for binary data. I have declared them as ordered and used WLSMV. The scaled robust fit indices are good (CFI, TLI and RMSEA). The robust statistics (in lines) suggest that the model does not fit the data. Which is better/more reliable for binary data?

Maria

niedziela, 5 lutego 2023 o 17:22:07 UTC+1 yros...@gmail.com napisał(a):
> On 2/3/23 23:18, Maria Cyniak-Cieciura wrote:
> > I have three questions referring to this situation.
> > 1) Is it ok to use WLSM and its robust statistics in such situation?
>
> I am afraid not. But the WLSMV 'scaled' versions are not ok either. See
>
> Savalei, V. (2021) Improving Fit Indices In SEM with categorical data.
> Multivariate Behavioral Research, 56(3), 390-407.
>
> > 2) in the case of MLM and MLMV point robust fit indices are the same and
> > there is a possibility to correct the RMSEA CIs and use robust fit
> > indices with MLMV. Is this also a case with WLSMV?
>
> In the last version of lavaan (0.6-13), we implemented the Savalei
> (2021) method for handling categorical data. This seems to be the best
> method we have for the moment. But it is only available for models
> without covariates or any other continuous variables. This should result
> in 'Robust' values for CFI and RMSEA.
>

messages.subject: Solving the Error in drawParam
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am working on a Power Analysis helping one professor of mine. I follow the tutorial from the Donnelly et al.
We have run a preliminary study, we have collected some standardized betas and we now use them in the model to find based on the them the sample we need for a power above 80%.

Our model is a moderated mediation one (similar to the one reported in the paper). Yet, when we put our parameters instead of those in the paper we receive the "Error in draw Param".

At some point Pr. Jorgensen mentioned in another discussion: "If you are getting that drawParam() error, perhaps you need to specify standardized parameters more carefully.  The tutorial shows how to use the simsem::find*() functions to find the residual variance that would make the total variance 1.  Making sure your explained variance is not > 1 can prevent the drawParam() error."

Yet, I am not sure how to use it. The code I have is for simplicity the same as Donnelly et al., (with just some different names)

N.per.group <- 25 # balanced group sample sizes
designMatrix <- expand.grid(X = 1:0, W = 1:0)
designMatrix$XW <- designMatrix$X * designMatrix$W # interaction
exoData <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:N.per.group, function(i)designMatrix))
a.w0 <- .5 # effect of X on M when moderator (W) == 0
 a.mod <- .3 # how much "a" path is moderated by W (i.e., interaction)
 b.w0 <- .4 # effect of M on Y when moderator (W) == 0
b.mod <- 0 # no moderating effect on "b" path
 c.w0 <- .2 # effect of X on Y when moderator (W) == 0
c.mod <- 0 # no moderating effect on "c" path
 w.M <- .1 # simple effect of moderator (W) on M when X == 0
 w.Y <- -.1 # simple effect of moderator (W) on Y when X == 0
 kappa.free <- kappa.pop <- matrix(NA, # estimate all effects
      nrow = 2, # 2 outcomes (M and Y)
      ncol = 3, # dummy coded X, W, XW
      dimnames = list(c("M","Y"),
      names(exoData)))
kappa.free["M","X"] <- "a.w0" # label free parameters
kappa.free["M","W"] <- "w.M" # (to define indirect effects)
kappa.free["M","XW"] <- "a.mod"
kappa.free["Y","X"] <- "c.w0"
kappa.free["Y","W" "w.Y"
kappa.free["Y","XW"] <- 0 # fixed to 0; label “c.mod” to free

kappa.pop["M","X"] <- a.w0 # set population parameters
kappa.pop["M","W"] <- w.M # (defined above)
kappa.pop["M","XW"] <- a.mod
kappa.pop["Y","X"] <- c.w0
kappa.pop["Y","W"] <- w.Y
kappa.pop["Y","XW"] <- c.mod

exoPaths <- bind(free = kappa.free, popParam = kappa.pop)

beta.free <- beta.pop <- matrix(0, nrow = 2, ncol = 2,
        dimnames = list(c("M","Y"), c("M","Y")))
beta.free["Y", "M"] <- "b"
beta.pop["Y", "M"] <- b.w0

endoPaths <- bind(free = beta.free, popParam = beta.pop)

residCor <- binds(free = diag(as.numeric(NA), 2), popParam = diag(2))

userParams <- ' ## conditional indirect effects
ind.w0 := a.w0 * b
ind.w1 := (a.w0 + a.mod) * b
## Test H0: equivalent indirect effects across W
ind.diff := a.mod * b
## or equivalently:
# ind.diff := ind.w1 – ind.w0 '

modMed1 <- model.path(BE = endoPaths, RPS = residCor,
                       KA = exoPaths, con = userParams, indLab = rownames(kappa.free),
                       covLab = colnames(kappa.free))
sim1 <- sim(nRep = 100, model = modMed1, covData = exoData,
                        n = nrow(exoData), seed = 777, outfun = rejectMCCI,
                        meanstructure = FALSE) # pass this argument to lavaan

set.seed(355)
 datmod <- generate(modMed1, covData = exoData, n = nrow(exoData))

Thank you in advance for any comment or help.
Best,
JP

messages.subject: Re: se = "bootstrap" and fixed.x
messages.body_plain:
We should also make a distinction between using the bootstrap to assess
the variability of point estimates (ie, standard error) on the one hand,
and using the bootstrap to compute a p-value for testing a hypothesis.

I believe that for the former case (standard errors), there should be no
difference between fixed.x = TRUE or fixed.x = FALSE, as the x-structure
is always saturated, and the point estimates for the regression
coefficients will always be the same. (Note that in linear regression,
fixed.x = TRUE is the default, even if the sampling model clearly
dictates that the x-values should change across samples. We use fixed.x
= TRUE anyway because it doesn't matter and it is much more convenient.)

In the latter case (p-value), we need to transform the data (eg using
the Bollen-Stine approach) so that it aligns with the null hypothesis.
In the regression world, this is what they do when they bootstrap the
(model-based) residuals.

Yves.

Observations 909

TLI .987 / .964

I was happy to receive such good statistics and also the bootstrapping of 5000 samples to get the CI for direct and indirect effects went smoothly (as far as I can tell), despite the low ratio of model parameters to observations.

a) It might also have something to do with the update and discovered bug in the versions < 0.6-13

Hello,

I'm running into an odd issue where I cannot get the residuals to constrain using the group.equal command.

I am doing a classic measurement invariance  procedure. Everything is working well until I get to comparing scalar invariance to strict invariance (which is including constraining the residuals across the two groups).

# Model syntax
model2 <- 'RGPTSA =~ A1 + A2 + A3 + A4 + A5 + A6 + A7 + A8
          RGPTSB =~ B1 + B2 + B3 + B4 + B5 + B6 + B7 + B8 + B9 + B10
          RGPTSA ~~ RGPTSB'

# scalar models
cfa.scalar <- cfa(model2, data = Passed_df, estimator = "WLSMV", group = "DEM_race", group.equal = c("loadings","intercepts"))

# strict model
cfa.strict <- cfa(model2, data = Passed_df, estimator = "WLSMV", group = "DEM_race", group.equal = c("loadings","intercepts", "residuals"))

This code is resulting in  identical models. I'm confused why the residuals being added to the group.equal is not constraining those parameters.

Any thoughts would be greatly appreciated.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jill,

Did you get any warning message when doing bootstrapping? Though artificial, I created an artificial case that can produce a similar problem:

# Adapted from https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/mediation.html
library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-14
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
set.seed(1235)
n <- 50
sigma <- lav_matrix_lower2full(c(1.00,
                                  .99, 1.00,
                                  .99,  .99, 1.00), diagonal = TRUE)
Data <- data.frame(MASS::mvrnorm(n, c(X = 0, M = 0, Y = 0), sigma, empirical = TRUE))
cov(Data)
#>      X    M    Y
#> X 1.00 0.99 0.99
#> M 0.99 1.00 0.99
#> Y 0.99 0.99 1.00
cor(Data)
#>      X    M    Y
#> X 1.00 0.99 0.99
#> M 0.99 1.00 0.99
#> Y 0.99 0.99 1.00
model <- ' # direct effect
             Y ~ c*X
           # mediator
             M ~ a*X
             Y ~ b*M

           # indirect effect (a*b)
             ab := a*b

           # total effect

             total := c + (a*b)
         '

fit <- sem(model, data = Data, se = "bootstrap", bootstrap = 100, iseed = 9)
#> Warning in lav_model_nvcov_bootstrap(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats =
#> lavsamplestats, : lavaan WARNING: 1 bootstrap runs failed or did not converge.

parameterEstimates(fit, boot.ci.type = "perc")

#>     lhs op     rhs label   est    se      z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
#> 1     Y  ~       X     c 0.497 0.092  5.398      0    0.342    0.730
#> 2     M  ~       X     a 0.990 0.015 65.506      0    0.957    1.017
#> 3     Y  ~       M     b 0.497 0.097  5.144      0    0.259    0.672

#> 7    ab :=     a*b    ab 0.493    NA     NA     NA    0.257    0.655
#> 8 total := c+(a*b) total 0.990    NA     NA     NA    0.963    1.020

I know the source of the problem in this artificial case. At least one bootstrap run had problem and this affects the computation of VCOV and hence the SEs for ab and total. However, CIs are computed differently and so are not affected.

Your case may be different but this may give some hints on what happened.

How about setting the seed for random number (iseed) when calling sem(), such that the results due to bootstrapping are reproducible? If the source of the problem is similar, you should have the NA problem only for some numbers of iseed. If this is due to random sampling in bootstrapping, then this can also explain why the NA problem only occurred in some runs. The randomness of the problem may not be due to computers or OSes, but due to the random sampling.

-- Shu Fai

Below is my code (note that given the number of items I have, the "model specification" part is abridged):

Model specification
general.factor =~

Nat_Corr_13_AN_1237_01_hf012 +
Nat_Corr_24_AN_1242_01_hf028 +
Nat_Corr_25_AN_0542_01_hf015 +
... (and so on for 132 items)

factor.1 =~ 22 items

factor.4 =~ 22 items
factor.5 =~ 22 items
factor.6 =~ 22 items

Running the CFA
mod.bifactor <- cfa(bifactor.model, data = df.newstudy, ordered = TRUE, orthogonal = TRUE, estimator = "WLSMV")

Below is the error I get when I run this model, and I can't get any fit measures or parameter estimates (any attempt to do so brings up a message telling me the model didn't converge):

lavaan WARNING: the optimizer (NLMINB) claimed the model converged,
                  but not all elements of the gradient are (near) zero;
                  the optimizer may not have found a local solution
                  use check.gradient = FALSE to skip this check.

I noticed that I get the same error when I specify a unidimensional model with all 132 items loading onto one factor. This error does not occur when I run a six-factor model with only the specific factors, so it looks like there's some sort of issue with that more general factor.

I found a previous post where someone had the same error, and the advice given was to look at potential model identification issues--but I don't think the model is underidentified. Is there anything about categorical data/use of polychoric correlations that inflates the likelihood of nonconvergence?

Please let me know if any additional information is required. Thanks!

Louisa

messages.subject: Order of model comparisons in lavTestLRT for measurement invariance
messages.subject_clean: Order of model comparisons in lavTestLRT for measurement invariance
messages.body_plain:
The documentation for lavTestLRT reads that it returns: "...When given a sequence of objects, this function tests the models against one another in the order specified." I am wondering if that is consistently true, particularly in the case of measurement invariance testing?

My context: I've scripted four dyadic invariance models (configural, loading, intercept, residual), however, rather than what we might call a "tear down" approach (where we start with the most unparsimonious model as baseline, and incrementally "tear it down" to whatever level of parsimony [invariance] is supported), I'd like to pursue a "build up" approach (starting with the most parsimonious model as baseline, and incrementally "building it up" to whatever level of complexity [noninvariance] is necessary). I don't think my models or reasons for desiring this approach are particularly important to answering the question here, but I can provide them if folks think they are germane.

The problem: when I actually run the nested model comparisons, lavTestLRT/anova are indifferent to the order that I specify. That is the following four lines all generate the same order of output:

anova(sat.config.fit, sat.loading.fit, sat.intercept.fit, sat.residual.fit)
anova(sat.residual.fit, sat.intercept.fit, sat.loading.fit, sat.config.fit)

lavTestLRT(sat.config.fit, sat.loading.fit, sat.intercept.fit, sat.residual.fit)
lavTestLRT(sat.residual.fit, sat.intercept.fit, sat.loading.fit, sat.config.fit)

The output consistently has the configural model as the topmost/first model in the output, followed by the loading, followed by the intercept, followed by the residual (I suspect it's just ordering from least : greatest df).

At the risk of embarrassing myself (as I find myself questioning things I took for granted), is the "build up" approach in this case not valid with the LRT approach? (i.e., is there some reason testing *decreases* in X^2 is logically incoherent/bad form?)

And if not, is there some secret sauce to getting lavTestLRT to compare the models in the sequence I desire. I am not opposed to writing my own boutique function to serve this purpose (if it's a reasonable testing approach), but it would be preferable if I didn't have to.

              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit.config     <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, group = "school")
fit.loadings   <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, group = "school", group.equal = c("loadings"))
fit.intercepts <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, group = "school", group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts"))
fit.residuals  <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, group = "school", group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts", "residuals"))

res <- lavTestLRT(fit.config, fit.loadings, fit.intercepts, fit.residuals)

res[order(-res$Df),]

> fit.residuals  <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, group = "school", group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts", "residuals"))

> Von: lav...@googlegroups.com <lav...@googlegroups.com> im Auftrag von John Sakaluk <jksa...@gmail.com>
> Gesendet: Freitag, 17. Februar 2023 14:24
> An: lavaan <lav...@googlegroups.com>
> Betreff: Order of model comparisons in lavTestLRT for measurement invariance
>
> The documentation for lavTestLRT reads that it returns: "...When given a sequence of objects, this function tests the models against one another in the order specified." I am wondering if that is consistently true, particularly in the case of measurement invariance testing?
>
> My context: I've scripted four dyadic invariance models (configural, loading, intercept, residual), however, rather than what we might call a "tear down" approach (where we start with the most unparsimonious model as baseline, and incrementally "tear it down" to whatever level of parsimony [invariance] is supported), I'd like to pursue a "build up" approach (starting with the most parsimonious model as baseline, and incrementally "building it up" to whatever level of complexity [noninvariance] is necessary). I don't think my models or reasons for desiring this approach are particularly important to answering the question here, but I can provide them if folks think they are germane.
>
> The problem: when I actually run the nested model comparisons, lavTestLRT/anova are indifferent to the order that I specify. That is the following four lines all generate the same order of output:
>
> anova(sat.config.fit, sat.loading.fit, sat.intercept.fit, sat.residual.fit)
> anova(sat.residual.fit, sat.intercept.fit, sat.loading.fit, sat.config.fit)
>

> lavTestLRT(sat.residual.fit, sat.intercept.fit, sat.loading.fit, sat.config.fit)
>

>

>
> And if not, is there some secret sauce to getting lavTestLRT to compare the models in the sequence I desire. I am not opposed to writing my own boutique function to serve this purpose (if it's a reasonable testing approach), but it would be preferable if I didn't have to.
>

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Shu Fai. It definitely does seem to be related to getting the warning that some of the bootstrap samples didn't iterate. Everyone of my students (N = 27) today had this problem. They all had just downloaded lavaan, so I think we can rule out lavaan version as a source of the problem. The R versions might have varied, but I know my version is up to date on both computers. I gathered OS information, and most students were using MacOS Monterey (12.4-12.6.3), but students using Ventura (13.2), which is the newest one, or BigSur (11.6), which is older also had that problem. In addition, for students using PCs, the problem emerged with Windows 10 and 11. That's a wide range of OS, so I don't think OS can be the source. I thought perhaps it was occurring only with laptops, which often have less memory, etc., because I didn't have the problem anymore when I switched from my Mac laptop to my iMac, but a student also had it happen on the PC desktop in the lab room.

One student discovered that it didn't happen when she used the lavaan() function with auto.var = TRUE instead of the sem() syntax listed in my original email, but that was true only when she dropped the se = "bootstrap" argument. As long as students had the se = "bootstrap" argument, the NAs appeared either in lavaan() or sem(). Can you tell me what difference that makes? What would lavaan be using for the se if there's no = "bootstrap", but the # of bootstrap samples argument is included, and in the parameterEstimates, we include the bootstrap type argument? I wasn't sure if the confidence intervals being reported would be from the percentile bootstraps or calculated not from bootstraps. Also, I also wasn't sure if the the z and p values would change if the se weren't coming from the bootstrap samples.

Thanks for your help,
Jill

messages.subject: simsem and MG-CFA simulation
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I'm using the package simsem on a simulation study looking at measurement invariance for ordinal data.  I'm using the lavaan syntax specification and relying heavily on the following two vignettes provided on the simsem website:

https://github.com/simsem/simsem/blob/master/SupportingDocs/Examples/Version05/ex6/ex6.R

https://github.com/simsem/simsem/blob/master/SupportingDocs/Examples/Version05/exMultipleFormat/ordered.R

 I noticed with the multiple group syntax, there is an error when I run it. I changed the rep count to 100 instead of 1000 and group size from 200 to 100,  and there is an extra replication added, so instead of 100 reps, there are 101 reps. Here is the syntax:

library(simsem)

 # The simulateData function still has a bug in setting multiple-group parameters

# Thus, in this example, the population data of each group are created manually and are fed to the sim function.

 # a) Noninvariance

 popNoninvariance1 <- "

f1 =~ 0.7*y1 + 0.7*y2 + 0.7*y3 + 0.7*y4 + 0.7*y5 + 0.7*y6

f1 ~~ 1*f1

y1 ~~ 0.51*y1

y2 ~~ 0.51*y2

y3 ~~ 0.51*y3

y4 ~~ 0.51*y4

y5 ~~ 0.51*y5

y6 ~~ 0.51*y6

f1 ~ 0*1

y1 ~ -0.2*1

y2 ~ -0.1*1

y3 ~ 0*1

y4 ~ 0.1*1

y5 ~ 0.2*1

y6 ~ 0.3*1

"

 popNoninvariance2 <- "

f1 =~ 0.7*y1 + 0.7*y2 + 0.7*y3

f2 =~ 0.7*y4 + 0.7*y5 + 0.7*y6

f1 ~~ 1*f1

f2 ~~ 1*f2

f1 ~~ 0.5*f2

y1 ~~ 0.51*y1

y2 ~~ 0.51*y2

y3 ~~ 0.51*y3

y4 ~~ 0.51*y4

y5 ~~ 0.51*y5

y6 ~~ 0.51*y6

f1 ~ 0*1

f2 ~ 0*1

y1 ~ 0.2*1

y2 ~ 0.1*1

y3 ~ 0*1

y4 ~ -0.1*1

y5 ~ -0.2*1

y6 ~ -0.3*1

"

# Population data are created with 100 cases in each group

 popDataNoninvariance1 <- simulateData(popNoninvariance1, sample.nobs = 100)

popDataNoninvariance2 <- simulateData(popNoninvariance2, sample.nobs = 100)

popDataNoninvariance <- rbind(popDataNoninvariance1, popDataNoninvariance2)

popDataNoninvariance <- data.frame(popDataNoninvariance, group = rep(c(1, 2), each = 100))

 analyzeNoninvariance <- "

f1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3

f2 =~ y4 + y5 + y6

f1 ~~ 1*f1

f2 ~~ 1*f2

f1 ~~ c(1, NA)*f2

y1 ~~ y1

y2 ~~ y2

y3 ~~ y3

y4 ~~ y4

y5 ~~ y5

y6 ~~ y6

f1 ~ 0*1

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have conducted a multigroup CFA that fitted well and demonstrated scalar invariance. In the configural model, some model parameters (e.g., factor loadings, item thresholds) exhibited interesting group differences that I would like to closely examine.

For instance, I am interested in knowing why the loading (or item threshold) for an item is higher in one group versus another, by treating the item loading as an outcome variable and regressing it on a number of other variables that I think might explain the group differences.

Is this a reasonable analysis in SEM and doable in lavaan? If not, are there other analyses that may help me answer these sorts of questions?

Appreciate it!
Frank

messages.body_plain:
Hi John,

no, I do not have a GH account. You don't have to mention me there. That's perfectly fine.

A note on lavTestLRT: apparently lavTestLRT only compares the model with the model that has the closest df distance. It would be great if there was an option to compare a model to all nested models. Amos does that (or did, I don't use Amos anymore). A (pointless) example: lavTestLRT compares the configural model to the model with constrained regressions model, but not to the model with constrained regressions and intercepts, even though the latter model is also nested within the configural model. Okay, the example makes little sense, but there are perfectly reasonable applications from my point of view. Maybe you can mention that as well?

Best

Christian

If I do, do you have a GH account (happy to credit you in the issue comment for the base-friendly reversal code)?

> I guess to be more clear, I am asking two questions, each of a different sort:
>
> 1. A more technical package functionality-oriented question: The language in the documentation for lavTestLRT states: "When given a sequence of objects, this function tests the models against one another in the order specified."  I am asking, therefore, whether the documentation is in err (or if it's not in err, if this is a minor bug for lavTestLRT, if it ought to be providing the reverse-ordered output given my reverse-order of specified models)? And:
> 2. A more substantive application question: I am asking whether this "build-up" approach is statistically/logically valid? I was pretty confident it was, but that lavTestLRT insisted on the "tear down" arrangement of output regardless of model order specified  had me second guessing myself.
>
> Your solution for reordering the output is effective and efficient but I wasn't so much worried about whether I could reorder the output, inasmuch as I was wondering whether, given the documentation, lavTestLRT ought to already be doing this given my specified order (question 1), and whether even if I could reorganize the table in code, whether this altered order was a valid testing procedure (question 2).
>

> > Betreff: Order of model comparisons in lavTestLRT for measurement invariance
> >
> > The documentation for lavTestLRT reads that it returns: "...When given a sequence of objects, this function tests the models against one another in the order specified." I am wondering if that is consistently true, particularly in the case of measurement invariance testing?
> >
> > My context: I've scripted four dyadic invariance models (configural, loading, intercept, residual), however, rather than what we might call a "tear down" approach (where we start with the most unparsimonious model as baseline, and incrementally "tear it down" to whatever level of parsimony [invariance] is supported), I'd like to pursue a "build up" approach (starting with the most parsimonious model as baseline, and incrementally "building it up" to whatever level of complexity [noninvariance] is necessary). > >

> >
> > At the risk of embarrassing myself (as I find myself questioning things I took for granted), is the "build up" approach in this case not valid with the LRT approach? (i.e., is there some reason testing *decreases* in X^2 is logically incoherent/bad form?)

messages.body_plain:
I will try to explain what *might* have happened, based on my limited understanding. Other members please correct me if I am wrong.

1) Are the CIs bootstrap CIs?

We can rule out the possibility that the CIs are normal theory CIs based on SE by checking whether the CIs are symmetric about the point estimates.

Using my previous example (https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/f1l5YOtlIrU/m/Wa67wTZ0DgAJ):

parameterEstimates(fit, boot.ci.type = "perc")
#>     lhs op     rhs label   est    se      z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
#> 1     Y  ~       X     c 0.497 0.092  5.398      0    0.342    0.730
#> 2     M  ~       X     a 0.990 0.015 65.506      0    0.957    1.017
#> 3     Y  ~       M     b 0.497 0.097  5.144      0    0.259    0.672
#> 4     Y ~~       Y       0.015 0.003  4.618      0    0.008    0.020
#> 5     M ~~       M       0.020 0.004  4.904      0    0.012    0.026
#> 6     X ~~       X       0.980 0.000     NA     NA    0.980    0.980
#> 7    ab :=     a*b    ab 0.493    NA     NA     NA    0.257    0.655
#> 8 total := c+(a*b) total 0.990    NA     NA     NA    0.963    1.020

If the CIs are based on SE, then they must be symmetric. That is, their distances from the point estimates (est) are the same. If they are not and you set se = "bootstrap" and ask for boot.ci <http://boot.ci>, they should be bootstrap CIs.

For my example:

est <- parameterEstimates(fit, boot.ci.type = "perc")
abs(est$ci.lower - est$est)
#> [1] 0.155503344 0.033346802 0.238254959 0.006786193 0.007784402 0.000000000
#> [7] 0.235291385 0.027343440
abs(est$ci.upper - est$est)
#> [1] 0.232163895 0.027023086 0.174776320 0.005492289 0.006801941 0.000000000
#> [7] 0.162719272 0.029812472

They are not symmetric about the point estimates. They are bootstrap CIs, as expected.

If I did not ask for bootstrapping, this is the result:

fit <- sem(model, data = Data)

parameterEstimates(fit, boot.ci.type = "perc")
#>     lhs op     rhs label   est    se      z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper

#> 1     Y  ~       X     c 0.497 0.123  4.055      0    0.257    0.738
#> 2     M  ~       X     a 0.990 0.020 49.624      0    0.951    1.029
#> 3     Y  ~       M     b 0.497 0.123  4.055      0    0.257    0.738
#> 4     Y ~~       Y       0.015 0.003  5.000      0    0.009    0.020
#> 5     M ~~       M       0.020 0.004  5.000      0    0.012    0.027

#> 6     X ~~       X       0.980 0.000     NA     NA    0.980    0.980

#> 7    ab :=     a*b    ab 0.493 0.122  4.042      0    0.254    0.731
#> 8 total := c+(a*b) total 0.990 0.020 49.624      0    0.951    1.029
est <- parameterEstimates(fit, boot.ci.type = "perc")
abs(est$ci.lower - est$est)
#> [1] 0.240446325 0.039101159 0.240446325 0.005752642 0.007644644 0.000000000
#> [7] 0.238835344 0.039101159
abs(est$ci.upper - est$est)
#> [1] 0.240446325 0.039101159 0.240446325 0.005752642 0.007644644 0.000000000
#> [7] 0.238835344 0.039101159

They are not symmetric about the point estimates. They are not bootstrap CIs.

2) Why NAs for SE and z but bootstrap CIs available?

My guess is, when computing bootstrap SEs for user-defined parameters, NAs are not removed. Therefore, if NAs are present in any of the bootstrap samples, it returns NAs for SEs and hence also for z and pvalue.

However, NAs are removed when forming percentile bootstrap CIs. Percentile bootstrap CI does not need SE and so it can return percentile bootstrap CIs even when SEs are NAs.

This usually is not an issue. If we prefer percentile bootstrap CIs to z-based CI, as for indirect effects, then it means that we allow for asymmetry in the sampling distribution. The SEs and p-values are not so useful. Actually, in the case of indirect effects, the p-values based on bootstrap SEs should not be interpreted, in my opinion, if we prefer using percentile (or BCa) bootstrap CIs.

3) How to check whether NAs in SEs are really due to NAs in bootstrap samples?

We can extract the bootstrap estimates using lavInspect and ask for "boot":

fit_boot <- lavInspect(fit, "boot")

Two attributes, "error.idx" and "nonadmissible", are relevant. "error.idx" stores the index of bootstrap samples the encountered error for whatever reasons.

In my example, estimates are NAs in one of the bootstrap samples (the 12th bootstrap sample)

(error.idx <- attr(fit_boot, "error.idx"))
#> [1] 12
(nonad <- attr(fit_boot, "nonadmissible"))
#> integer(0)

These are the estimates in the 10th to 14th bootstrap samples:

fit_boot[sort(c(error.idx - 1:2, error.idx, error.idx + 1:2)), ]
#>              c         a         b       Y~~Y       M~~M
#> [1,] 0.6305563 0.9740943 0.3755701 0.01131400 0.02023379
#> [2,] 0.4621861 0.9868740 0.5601131 0.01203450 0.01634239
#> [3,]        NA        NA        NA         NA         NA
#> [4,] 0.3801079 0.9639834 0.6537283 0.01060975 0.01427636
#> [5,] 0.4485607 0.9834801 0.5577716 0.00878299 0.01543722

If you see NAs in SEs, you can check whether there are NAs in some bootstrap samples. If yes, then this may explain why you see NAs in the SEs.

Note that these NAs in bootstrap samples may be "natural" and "normal." Bootstrapping involves randomly sampling. Therefore, even if a model has no problem in estimation when fitting to the full sample, problems can occur in some random bootstrap samples.

4) Setting iseed when asking for bootstrapping CIs.

When doing bootstrapping, regardless of the programs used (PROCESS, lavaan, etc.), I usually set the seed for the random number generator. In lavaan, this can be done using iseed (note that iseed does not work in some previous versions, so make sure you use the latest version of lavaan):

fit <- sem(model, data = Data, se = "bootstrap", bootstrap = 5000, iseed = 9)

This allows us to produce the same set of bootstrap samples across platforms, as long as the random number generator is the same across platforms.

In your case, you can try to set the iseed to some numbers and do the analysis. If the NA problem occurs when setting iseed to a number, the same problem should occur also in other platform. On the other hand, if the NA problem does not occur for a number, then you should see no NA in other platforms if you set iseed to the same number.

Hope this helps.

-- Shu Fai

> I will try to explain what *might* have happened, based on my limited understanding. Other members please correct me if I am wrong.
>
> 1) Are the CIs bootstrap CIs?
>
> We can rule out the possibility that the CIs are normal theory CIs based on SE by checking whether the CIs are symmetric about the point estimates.
>
> Using my previous example (https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/f1l5YOtlIrU/m/Wa67wTZ0DgAJ):
>
> parameterEstimates(fit, boot.ci.type = "perc")

> #> 8 total := c+(a*b) total 0.990    NA     NA     NA    0.963    1.020
>
> If the CIs are based on SE, then they must be symmetric. That is, their distances from the point estimates (est) are the same. If they are not and you set se = "bootstrap" and ask for boot.ci <http://boot.ci>, they should be bootstrap CIs.
>
> For my example:
>
> est <- parameterEstimates(fit, boot.ci.type = "perc")
> abs(est$ci.lower - est$est)
> #> [1] 0.155503344 0.033346802 0.238254959 0.006786193 0.007784402 0.000000000

> #> [7] 0.162719272 0.029812472

> They are not symmetric about the point estimates. They are bootstrap CIs, as expected.

> If I did not ask for bootstrapping, this is the result:

> fit <- sem(model, data = Data)

> parameterEstimates(fit, boot.ci.type = "perc")

>

> #> 7    ab :=     a*b    ab 0.493 0.122  4.042      0    0.254    0.731
> #> 8 total := c+(a*b) total 0.990 0.020 49.624      0    0.951    1.029
> est <- parameterEstimates(fit, boot.ci.type = "perc")

> #> [7] 0.238835344 0.039101159
>
> They are not symmetric about the point estimates. They are not bootstrap CIs.
>
> 2) Why NAs for SE and z but bootstrap CIs available?
>
> My guess is, when computing bootstrap SEs for user-defined parameters, NAs are not removed. Therefore, if NAs are present in any of the bootstrap samples, it returns NAs for SEs and hence also for z and pvalue.
>
> However, NAs are removed when forming percentile bootstrap CIs. Percentile bootstrap CI does not need SE and so it can return percentile bootstrap CIs even when SEs are NAs.
>
> This usually is not an issue. If we prefer percentile bootstrap CIs to z-based CI, as for indirect effects, then it means that we allow for asymmetry in the sampling distribution. The SEs and p-values are not so useful. Actually, in the case of indirect effects, the p-values based on bootstrap SEs should not be interpreted, in my opinion, if we prefer using percentile (or BCa) bootstrap CIs.
>
> 3) How to check whether NAs in SEs are really due to NAs in bootstrap samples?
>
> We can extract the bootstrap estimates using lavInspect and ask for "boot":
>
> fit_boot <- lavInspect(fit, "boot")
>
> Two attributes, "error.idx" and "nonadmissible", are relevant. "error.idx" stores the index of bootstrap samples the encountered error for whatever reasons.
>
> In my example, estimates are NAs in one of the bootstrap samples (the 12th bootstrap sample)
>
> (error.idx <- attr(fit_boot, "error.idx"))
> #> [1] 12
> (nonad <- attr(fit_boot, "nonadmissible"))
> #> integer(0)
>
> These are the estimates in the 10th to 14th bootstrap samples:
>
> fit_boot[sort(c(error.idx - 1:2, error.idx, error.idx + 1:2)), ]
> #>              c         a         b       Y~~Y       M~~M
> #> [1,] 0.6305563 0.9740943 0.3755701 0.01131400 0.02023379
> #> [2,] 0.4621861 0.9868740 0.5601131 0.01203450 0.01634239
> #> [3,]        NA        NA        NA         NA         NA
> #> [4,] 0.3801079 0.9639834 0.6537283 0.01060975 0.01427636
> #> [5,] 0.4485607 0.9834801 0.5577716 0.00878299 0.01543722
>
> If you see NAs in SEs, you can check whether there are NAs in some bootstrap samples. If yes, then this may explain why you see NAs in the SEs.
>
> Note that these NAs in bootstrap samples may be "natural" and "normal." Bootstrapping involves randomly sampling. Therefore, even if a model has no problem in estimation when fitting to the full sample, problems can occur in some random bootstrap samples.
>
> 4) Setting iseed when asking for bootstrapping CIs.
>
> When doing bootstrapping, regardless of the programs used (PROCESS, lavaan, etc.), I usually set the seed for the random number generator. In lavaan, this can be done using iseed (note that iseed does not work in some previous versions, so make sure you use the latest version of lavaan):
>
> fit <- sem(model, data = Data, se = "bootstrap", bootstrap = 5000, iseed = 9)
>
> This allows us to produce the same set of bootstrap samples across platforms, as long as the random number generator is the same across platforms.
>
> In your case, you can try to set the iseed to some numbers and do the analysis. If the NA problem occurs when setting iseed to a number, the same problem should occur also in other platform. On the other hand, if the NA problem does not occur for a number, then you should see no NA in other platforms if you set iseed to the same number.
>
> Hope this helps.
>
> -- Shu Fai

Correction again. I am not precise enough in my message. Sorry.

Percentile bootstrap CIs can be nearly symmetric about the point estimates, though they should not be *exactly* symmetric about the point estimates. CIs based on SEs are exactly symmetric about the point estimates.

And I meant "percentile bootstrap CIs" or similar CIs [e.g., BCa CIs] when I just wrote "bootstrap CIs". In my area, we rarely use bootstrap SEs to form symmetric CIs, though it can be done.

> > If the CIs are based on SE, then they must be symmetric. That is, their distances from the point estimates (est) are the same. If they are not and you set se = "bootstrap" and ask for boot.ci <http://boot.ci>, they should be bootstrap CIs.
> >
> > For my example:
> >
> > est <- parameterEstimates(fit, boot.ci.type = "perc")
> > abs(est$ci.lower - est$est)
> > #> [1] 0.155503344 0.033346802 0.238254959 0.006786193 0.007784402 0.000000000
> > #> [7] 0.235291385 0.027343440
> > abs(est$ci.upper - est$est)
> > #> [1] 0.232163895 0.027023086 0.174776320 0.005492289 0.006801941 0.000000000
> > #> [7] 0.162719272 0.029812472
> >
> > They are not symmetric about the point estimates. They are bootstrap CIs, as expected.
> >
> > If I did not ask for bootstrapping, this is the result:
> >
> > fit <- sem(model, data = Data)
> >
> > parameterEstimates(fit, boot.ci.type = "perc")
> > #>     lhs op     rhs label   est    se      z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
> > #> 1     Y  ~       X     c 0.497 0.123  4.055      0    0.257    0.738
> > #> 2     M  ~       X     a 0.990 0.020 49.624      0    0.951    1.029
> > #> 3     Y  ~       M     b 0.497 0.123  4.055      0    0.257    0.738
> > #> 4     Y ~~       Y       0.015 0.003  5.000      0    0.009    0.020
> > #> 5     M ~~       M       0.020 0.004  5.000      0    0.012    0.027
> >
> > #> 6     X ~~       X       0.980 0.000     NA     NA    0.980    0.980
> > #> 7    ab :=     a*b    ab 0.493 0.122  4.042      0    0.254    0.731
> > #> 8 total := c+(a*b) total 0.990 0.020 49.624      0    0.951    1.029
> > est <- parameterEstimates(fit, boot.ci.type = "perc")
> > abs(est$ci.lower - est$est)
> > #> [1] 0.240446325 0.039101159 0.240446325 0.005752642 0.007644644 0.000000000
> > #> [7] 0.238835344 0.039101159
> > abs(est$ci.upper - est$est)
> > #> [1] 0.240446325 0.039101159 0.240446325 0.005752642 0.007644644 0.000000000
> > #> [7] 0.238835344 0.039101159
> >
> > They are not symmetric about the point estimates. They are not bootstrap CIs.
> >
> > 2) Why NAs for SE and z but bootstrap CIs available?
> >
> > My guess is, when computing bootstrap SEs for user-defined parameters, NAs are not removed. Therefore, if NAs are present in any of the bootstrap samples, it returns NAs for SEs and hence also for z and pvalue.
> >
> > However, NAs are removed when forming percentile bootstrap CIs. Percentile bootstrap CI does not need SE and so it can return percentile bootstrap CIs even when SEs are NAs.
> >
> > This usually is not an issue. If we prefer percentile bootstrap CIs to z-based CI, as for indirect effects, then it means that we allow for asymmetry in the sampling distribution. The SEs and p-values are not so useful. Actually, in the case of indirect effects, the p-values based on bootstrap SEs should not be interpreted, in my opinion, if we prefer using percentile (or BCa) bootstrap CIs.
> >
> > 3) How to check whether NAs in SEs are really due to NAs in bootstrap samples?
> >
> > We can extract the bootstrap estimates using lavInspect and ask for "boot":
> >
> > fit_boot <- lavInspect(fit, "boot")
> >
> > Two attributes, "error.idx" and "nonadmissible", are relevant. "error.idx" stores the index of bootstrap samples the encountered error for whatever reasons.
> >
> > In my example, estimates are NAs in one of the bootstrap samples (the 12th bootstrap sample)
> >
> > (error.idx <- attr(fit_boot, "error.idx"))
> > #> [1] 12
> > (nonad <- attr(fit_boot, "nonadmissible"))
> > #> integer(0)
> >
> > These are the estimates in the 10th to 14th bootstrap samples:
> >
> > fit_boot[sort(c(error.idx - 1:2, error.idx, error.idx + 1:2)), ]
> > #>              c         a         b       Y~~Y       M~~M
> > #> [1,] 0.6305563 0.9740943 0.3755701 0.01131400 0.02023379
> > #> [2,] 0.4621861 0.9868740 0.5601131 0.01203450 0.01634239
> > #> [3,]        NA        NA        NA         NA         NA
> > #> [4,] 0.3801079 0.9639834 0.6537283 0.01060975 0.01427636
> > #> [5,] 0.4485607 0.9834801 0.5577716 0.00878299 0.01543722
> >
> > If you see NAs in SEs, you can check whether there are NAs in some bootstrap samples. If yes, then this may explain why you see NAs in the SEs.
> >
> > Note that these NAs in bootstrap samples may be "natural" and "normal." Bootstrapping involves randomly sampling. Therefore, even if a model has no problem in estimation when fitting to the full sample, problems can occur in some random bootstrap samples.
> >
> > 4) Setting iseed when asking for bootstrapping CIs.
> >
> > When doing bootstrapping, regardless of the programs used (PROCESS, lavaan, etc.), I usually set the seed for the random number generator. In lavaan, this can be done using iseed (note that iseed does not work in some previous versions, so make sure you use the latest version of lavaan):
> >
> > fit <- sem(model, data = Data, se = "bootstrap", bootstrap = 5000, iseed = 9)
> >
> > This allows us to produce the same set of bootstrap samples across platforms, as long as the random number generator is the same across platforms.
> >
> > In your case, you can try to set the iseed to some numbers and do the analysis. If the NA problem occurs when setting iseed to a number, the same problem should occur also in other platform. On the other hand, if the NA problem does not occur for a number, then you should see no NA in other platforms if you set iseed to the same number.

messages.subject: Re: se = "bootstrap" and fixed.x
messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Terrence and Yves, for your comments and advice. messages.subject: semfindr: Case influience on models fitted by lavaan
messages.subject_clean: semfindr: Case influience on models fitted by lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Hi lavaan Google group members;

I would like to share a package Mark Lai and I developed, semfindr, "finder", without the "e":

https://sfcheung.github.io/semfindr/

The stable release is available on CRAN. The latest developmental release can be installed from GitHub:

remotes::install_github("sfcheung/semfindr")

It has one main goal:

- Help identifying influential cases, if any, in models fitted by lavaan (for now).

It can compute most of the measures introduced by Pek and MacCallum (2011) in their excellent paper on sensitivity analysis in SEM:

- several kinds of case influence measure on parameters.
- generalized Cook's distance on all free parameters or a subset of free paramters of interest (e.g., all path coefficients).
- case influence on fit measures, mainly model chi-square but any fit measures reported by lavaan::fitMeasures() are supported.
- Generating plots of case influence measures.

There are other packages for doing these tasks. However, we have projects with large samples and/or models difficult to fit (e.g., big models with missing data). We would like to have something more efficient to use in these projects. Hence this package, developed partly to meet our own needs but maybe it can also serve other researchers.

It supports two approaches:

- The conventional leave-one-out approach, but this phase only needs to be done once, and can be done on selected cases. The stored results can be reused by other case influence functions, such that case influence can be examined as often as desired without refitting the model for each case.

- An approximate approach (only for ML estimator) that approximtes some case influence measures without the need to refitting the model for each case. The measure is not exact, but usually close enough in ranking and can be computed quickly.

These two approaches can be used together. E.g.. use the approximate approach first to identify a potential set of influential cases quickly, and then use the leave-one-out approach to compute the exact influence.

More on the basic features can be found in the Get Started vignette:

https://sfcheung.github.io/semfindr/articles/semfindr.html

It still has some limitations. For example, it does not yet support multisample models. But this is our priority because we also have studies with multisample models.

Comments and bug reports are much appreciated. They would be great for helping us to improve the package.

Hope you find semfindr useful.

-- Shu Fai

Reference:

Pek, J., & MacCallum, R. (2011). Sensitivity analysis in structural equation models: Cases and their influence. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 46(2), 202-228. https://doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2011.561068

messages.subject: Re: Order of model comparisons in lavTestLRT for measurement invariance
messages.subject_clean: Order of model comparisons in lavTestLRT for measurement invariance
messages.body_plain:
John,

You wrote:
>>>
2. A more substantive application question: I am asking whether this "build-up" approach is statistically/logically valid? I was pretty confident it was, but that lavTestLRT insisted on the "tear down" arrangement of output regardless of model order specified  had me second guessing myself.
>>>

I may be misunderstanding your question but Peter Bentler (2000), in the section on nested tests, stated that when you begin with the most general model and test the result of adding a constraint, the sequential tests are statistically independent of one another.  However, if you begin with the most restricted model and release constraints, this independence between successive tests does not hold.

Keith

Peter M. Bentler (2000) Rites, Wrongs, and Gold in Model Testing, Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal, 7:1, 82-91, DOI: 10.1207/S15328007SEM0701_04 <https://doi.org/10.1207/S15328007SEM0701_04>

------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/
