messages.subject: Re: bootstrapLavaan and standardized coefficients
messages.body_plain:
Hi Zheng,

Maybe the following example can give you some ideas. There are still things that need to be modified but I believe it is close to what you need.

```r
# Adapted from https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/mediation.html

# Set the width
opt_old <- options(width = 100)

library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-14
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
set.seed(1234)
X <- rnorm(100)
M <- 0.5*X + rnorm(100)
Y <- 0.7*M + rnorm(100)
Data <- data.frame(X = X, Y = Y, M = M)
model <- ' # direct effect
             Y ~ c*X
           # mediator
             M ~ a*X
             Y ~ b*M
           # indirect effect (a*b)
             ab := a*b
           # total effect
             total := c + (a*b)
         '
fit <- sem(model, data = Data)

# Write a function to extract the standardized estimates
get_std <- function(x, ...) {
    std <- lavaan::standardizedSolution(x, ...)
    std$est.std
  }

# Check the function
# Should equal to the column `est.std`
standardizedSolution(fit)
#>     lhs op     rhs label est.std    se      z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
#> 1     Y  ~       X     c   0.028 0.080  0.348  0.728   -0.128    0.184
#> 2     M  ~       X     a   0.419 0.079  5.319  0.000    0.265    0.573
#> 3     Y  ~       M     b   0.679 0.063 10.865  0.000    0.557    0.802
#> 4     Y ~~       Y         0.522 0.072  7.268  0.000    0.381    0.663
#> 5     M ~~       M         0.825 0.066 12.497  0.000    0.695    0.954
#> 6     X ~~       X         1.000 0.000     NA     NA    1.000    1.000
#> 7    ab :=     a*b    ab   0.285 0.062  4.619  0.000    0.164    0.405
#> 8 total := c+(a*b) total   0.312 0.088  3.548  0.000    0.140    0.485
get_std(fit)
#> [1] 0.02769268 0.41888560 0.67937899 0.52191562 0.82453486 1.00000000 0.28458207 0.31227475

# Do bootstrapping
# Set other arguments (e.g., ncpus, parallel, etc.) if necessary
# Increase R for the final results.
std_boot <- bootstrapLavaan(fit,
                            R = 500L,
                            FUN = get_std,
                            iseed = 1234)
# Inspect the estimates
head(std_boot)
#>             [,1]      [,2]      [,3]      [,4]      [,5] [,6]      [,7]      [,8]
#> [1,] -0.05174324 0.4539046 0.7189981 0.5141378 0.7939706    1 0.3263566 0.2746133
#> [2,]  0.02535236 0.4545628 0.7058346 0.4848863 0.7933727    1 0.3208462 0.3461985
#> [3,]  0.23895775 0.5102153 0.6013216 0.4346853 0.7396804    1 0.3068035 0.5457612
#> [4,]  0.03827328 0.4888300 0.6421786 0.5621126 0.7610452    1 0.3139162 0.3521895
#> [5,] -0.01751884 0.4111792 0.7357095 0.4690238 0.8309316    1 0.3025085 0.2849896
#> [6,] -0.02185791 0.6188300 0.7275512 0.4898736 0.6170494    1 0.4502305 0.4283726

# Form the percentile CIs
# Just a crude illustration.
# This is not exactly the method used by lavaan.
# I added na.rm = TRUE, in case the bootstrap
# estimates are NA in some bootstrap samples.
std_boot_ci <- t(apply(std_boot,
                       MARGIN = 2,
                       FUN = quantile,
                       probs = c(.025, .975),
                       na.rm = TRUE))
std_boot_ci
#>            2.5%     97.5%
#> [1,] -0.1424820 0.2019654
#> [2,]  0.2488895 0.5843217
#> [3,]  0.5007692 0.8066854
#> [4,]  0.3879182 0.6540134
#> [5,]  0.6585654 0.9380481
#> [6,]  1.0000000 1.0000000
#> [7,]  0.1690466 0.4063573
#> [8,]  0.1370658 0.4930246

# Append the CIs to lavaan output
std <- standardizedSolution(fit)
std[ c("ci.lower.boot", "ci.upper.boot")] <- std_boot_ci
std
#>     lhs op     rhs label est.std    se      z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper ci.lower.boot ci.upper.boot
#> 1     Y  ~       X     c   0.028 0.080  0.348  0.728   -0.128    0.184        -0.142         0.202
#> 2     M  ~       X     a   0.419 0.079  5.319  0.000    0.265    0.573         0.249         0.584
#> 3     Y  ~       M     b   0.679 0.063 10.865  0.000    0.557    0.802         0.501         0.807
#> 4     Y ~~       Y         0.522 0.072  7.268  0.000    0.381    0.663         0.388         0.654
#> 5     M ~~       M         0.825 0.066 12.497  0.000    0.695    0.954         0.659         0.938
#> 6     X ~~       X         1.000 0.000     NA     NA    1.000    1.000         1.000         1.000
#> 7    ab :=     a*b    ab   0.285 0.062  4.619  0.000    0.164    0.405         0.169         0.406
#> 8 total := c+(a*b) total   0.312 0.088  3.548  0.000    0.140    0.485         0.137         0.493

# Restore the width
options(opt_old)
```
Created on 2023-02-19 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)

I actually wrote a function to do something similar (https://sfcheung.github.io/semhelpinghands/articles/standardizedSolution_boot_ci.html). However, I did that mainly for a case I myself need, requesting bootstrap CIs for both the unstandardized and standardized solutions. As shown above, it is not difficult to DIY using bootstrapLavaan(), which you mentioned, without using other packages. Moreover, you can have more control on the processes. That's why I use bootstrapLavaan() above instead of that function I wrote.

Hope this helps.

Regards,
Shu Fai Cheung (張樹輝)

Is declaring factor indicators (or manifest variables in general) as censored not available in lavaan? And do we have a general overview over limitations in lavaan that cannot be handled by semTools or similar additional packages?

messages.body_plain:
My thanks as well, Keith.

In reading the Bentler piece, I am curious as to how he came to believe the independence did not hold with the "build up" testing sequence (i.e., starting with most restrictive). I've gone through Steiger et al. (1985) a few times now, and best I can tell (admittedly quite fallible because navigating proofs is decidedly not a long-suit of mine), I'm not under the impression that Steiger et al. indulged the "build up" order, but rather, it seems they exclusively focused on the "tear down" (i.e., starting with the least restrictive). At the very least, their Monte Carlo simulations seem exclusively focused on the latter. Of course, maybe Bentler did the simulations with the "build up" approach himself and found the independence established in Steiger et al did not hold (and that's what motivated the remark), but I'm left wondering where to find some more detail about the extent of the problem.

Still, really appreciate the very promising lead!

-John

messages.body_plain:
Seems this post has been unanswered for a week now... You deserve an answer!

- I would like to know if the two models are valid. Could I use the mod one with warning message?

You can look up negative error variance. It is not an admissible solution (variances cannot be negative; how could variation be negative...). Unfortunately, reading output in google groups is not easy unless you use a monospace font (like courier).

Your fist model results in a negative error variance for Max_Temperatur, this item is not included in your second model. A negative error variance might come from an item being a particularly strong indicator of a latent variable, but your point estimate is quite strong (and negative). Other causes of negative error variance include low sample size (not in your case) and using too few indicators of a latent variable (not in your case).

I think you should work further with your models. In addition to the negative error variance, both models have too low fit. I suggest reading on negative error variance (also referred to as Heywood cases) and model fit, and how to develop latent variables.

messages.subject: Scaling for measurement items
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have used 7 point scales for most of my measurements.
On one latent construct, I have three items
a) 7 point scale (EX01)
b) ruler with 101 steps (EX02)
c) 3 point scale (EX03) (closer to binary)

All three can potentially reflect one construct.

If I use the following statement in the measurement model.
Use =~ EX01 + EX02 + EX03

I get the following warning:
Warning message: In lav_data_full(data = data, group = group, cluster = cluster, : lavaan WARNING: some observed variances are (at least) a factor 1000 times larger than others; use varTable(fit) to investigate

I did run the varTable() and found that the the variance in EX02
EX01 mean  2.414   var 3.702
EX02 mean  32.940 var 1065.488
EX03 mean 1.750    var 0.903

Is there a good way to scale EX02 or all 3 to work around the variance issue?

Thanks for all replies !

Carsten

messages.subject: Model with multiple mediation/moderation effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to test the following model, and am curious if the code I have written is the appropriate way to represent these effects.  We are assuming that the moderators (Z and M) can affect the mediator (Y) and the DV.

Model:

Current code:
model <- '
# Regression equations
  M ~ aZ * Z + control_1 + control_2 + control_3

  Y ~ bM * M + bX * X + bXM * X:M + bZ * Z + bXZ * X:Z + control_1 + control_2 + control_3

  DV ~ cM * M + cX * X + cXM * X:M + cZ * Z + cXZ * X:Z + cY * Y + control_1 + control_2 + control_3

# Mean of X
  X ~ X.mean * 1

# Variance of X
  X ~~ X.var * X

# Effects on Mediator conditional on moderator
  ZtoM.SDlo := ( aZ )
  ZtoM.SDhi := ( aZ )

########## Y effects

# Indirect Effects Conditional on Moderator
  Y.indirect.SDlo := (bM + bXM * (X.mean - sqrt(X.var))) * ZtoM.SDlo
  Y.indirect.SDhi := (bM + bXM * (X.mean + sqrt(X.var))) * ZtoM.SDhi

# Index of Moderated Mediation
  index.mod.med: = ( aZ ) * bXM

# Covariance of Exogeneous Variables
  Enact_Condition ~~ Gender_code

# Direct Effects Conditional on Moderator
  Y.direct.SDlo := (bZ + bXZ * (X.mean - sqrt(X.var)))
  Y.direct.SDhi := (bZ + bXZ * (X.mean + sqrt(X.var)))

# Total Effects conditional on moderator
  Y.total.SDlo := Y.direct.SDlo + Y.indirect.SDlo
  Y.total.SDhi := Y.direct.SDhi + Y.indirect.SDhi

# Proportion Mediated Conditional on Moderator
  Y.prop.mediated.SDlo := Y.indirect.SDlo / Y.total.SDlo
  Y.prop.mediated.SDhi := Y.indirect.SDhi / Y.total.SDhi

########## DV effects

# Indirect Effects Conditional on Moderator (gender to belonging)
  DV.indirect.SDlo := (cX+ cY) * (bM + bXM * (X.mean - sqrt(X.var))) * ZtoM.SDlo
  DV.indirect.SDhi := (cX+ cY) * (bM + bXM * (X.mean + sqrt(X.var))) * ZtoM.SDhi

# Index of Moderated Mediation (alternativ test for sign. differences among different moderator levels)
  DV.index.mod.med: = ( aZ ) * bXM * cY

# Direct Effects Conditional on Moderator (gender to belonging)
  ZtoDV.direct.SDlo := (cZ + cXZ * (X.mean - sqrt(X.var)))
  ZtoDV.direct.SDhi := (cZ + cXZ * (X.mean + sqrt(X.var)))

# Direct Effects Conditional on Moderator (threat to belonging)
  MtoDV.direct.SDlo := (cM + cXM * (X.mean - sqrt(X.var)))
  MtoDV.direct.SDhi := (cM + cXM * (X.mean + sqrt(X.var)))

# Total Effects conditional on moderator
  DV.total.SDlo := ZtoDV.direct.SDlo + MtoDV.direct.SDlo + DV.indirect.SDlo
  DV.total.SDhi := ZtoDV.direct.SDhi + MtoDV.direct.SDhi + DV.indirect.SDhi

  # Proportion Mediated Conditional on Moderator (To match the output of mediate package)
  DV.prop.mediated.SDlo := DV.indirect.SDlo / DV.total.SDlo
  DV.prop.mediated.SDhi := DV.indirect.SDhi / DV.total.SDhi

'

model.fit <- sem(model = model,
                           data = data,
                           se = "bootstrap",
                           bootstrap = 500)

model.results <- parameterEstimates(model.fit,
                              boot.ci.type = "bca.simple",
                              level = .95, ci = TRUE,
                              standardized = FALSE)
model.results

I am also wondering if it would be possible to represent Z as a categorical variable with 4 categories, using 3 dummy variables, or if this would cause the calculations of the effects to be incorrect?

Alternatively, I am wondering if Z could be replaced with an interaction between two variables, as pictured below, or if this kind of model would be beyond the means of what lavaan can do?

Thank you very very much for your help!

messages.subject: Re: Scaling for measurement items
messages.body_plain:
Carsten,
You can find a detailed discussion of this issue in Kline's SEM text ("Relative Variances", Chapter 4). The short answer is that you can multiply or divide variables by a constant to modify the variance.  It is often convenient to stick to multiples of 10 to simply move the decimal to the left or right.

If you are using a unit loading constraint to fix the scale of the latent variable, you might want to consider using EX02 because it has more values and is likely to be more sensitive.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.body_plain:
Dear Gouvidé,

I checked your solution, and I have noted several issues that you might want to address in in improving your model:
1. As much as I see, you introduced covariances among items measuring F1 and F2. While this might be theoretically appropriate, I observed that correlations among these items (std. covariances) are larger than 1. This indicates problems.
2. I see that the error variances of the two items (Rainfall and Malaria_Incdience) is not statistically significant. While this might not necessarily be a reason for alarm, it is worth checking out. See Brown's 2015 book Confirmatory factor analysis for applied research page 114.
3. The F1 and F2 factors do NOT have a statistically significant influence on Malaria Incidence + this effect is very very different than the effect of your model 1 (which I think is the most reasonable model).
Based on these considerations, I would not trust your proposed solution.

Now, I do not know the conceptual underpinnings for the model and the need for two factors, however, could not the same aim be achieved by running OLS regression analysis with the items in factors F1 and F2 predicting malaria incidence? In this case, you might want to remove redundant items to avoid multicollinearity (e.g., by using principal components analysis to select the items that best represent each of your two factors; see Hair et al., Multivariate data analysis). It seems to me that the reason your model has problems is because the items in each factor are measuring almost the same thing (i.e., in F1 all measure some form of humidity, in F2 all measure some form of temperature).

Hope this helps,
Jošt

messages.subject: ML SEM
messages.body_plain:
Dear Lavaan Project Team,

While working on a multilevel SEM model with Lavaan, we encountered some problems.

Background: We run a multigroup SEM model across several countries. The results show that for one of the three latent variables we want to model, two indicators seem to be problematic.

Therefore, in the next step we want to find out via multilevel SEM whether these varying effects of individual indicators can be attributed to country differences. In concrete terms, our model looks as follows:

solidx <- '

level: 1

  local =~ v212r+v213r+v214r

  global =~ v215r+v216r+v219r

 social =~ v217r+v218r+v220r

  v217r~~v220r

  v219r~~v218r

  v212r~~v213r

level: 2

  local =~ v212r+v213r+v214r

  global =~ v215r+v216r+v219r

  social =~ v217r+v218r+v220r

  v215r~voteshare

  v215r~imm1

  v215r~GDP

  v215r~yearseu

  v219r~GDP

  v219r~voteshare

'

fit <- sem(model=solidx,data=evsdata_vera, cluster = "country")

summary(fit)

fitMeasures(fit)

Even though the model converges, we get the following error message:

In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :

  lavaan WARNING:

    The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov)

    does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue

    (= -7.463257e+07) is smaller than zero. This may be a symptom that

    the model is not identified.

Do you have an idea what is incorrect in our models or what needs to be corrected to eliminate this error? Moreover, some SE could not be computed.

All the best and many thanks,

Ann-Kathrin

> Dear Gouvidé,
>
> I checked your solution, and I have noted several issues that you might want to address in in improving your model:
> 1. As much as I see, you introduced covariances among items measuring F1 and F2. While this might be theoretically appropriate, I observed that correlations among these items (std. covariances) are larger than 1. This indicates problems.
> 2. I see that the error variances of the two items (Rainfall and Malaria_Incdience) is not statistically significant. While this might not necessarily be a reason for alarm, it is worth checking out. See Brown's 2015 book Confirmatory factor analysis for applied research page 114.
> 3. The F1 and F2 factors do NOT have a statistically significant influence on Malaria Incidence + this effect is very very different than the effect of your model 1 (which I think is the most reasonable model).
> Based on these considerations, I would not trust your proposed solution.
>
> Now, I do not know the conceptual underpinnings for the model and the need for two factors, however, could not the same aim be achieved by running OLS regression analysis with the items in factors F1 and F2 predicting malaria incidence? In this case, you might want to remove redundant items to avoid multicollinearity (e.g., by using principal components analysis to select the items that best represent each of your two factors; see Hair et al., Multivariate data analysis). It seems to me that the reason your model has problems is because the items in each factor are measuring almost the same thing (i.e., in F1 all measure some form of humidity, in F2 all measure some form of temperature).

Dear Ann-Kathrin,

I don't really see anything wrong with the model (others might!) but maybe we could get some basic troubleshooting out of the way?
What kind of sample size?
Have you tried using the EM optimizer as discussed here? https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/multilevel.html#convergence-issues-and-solutions
Have you tried a simpler model, perhaps with only a single regressor for v215r and v219r?
Possibly you've done all of these things already, just wanted to double-check.

As for the standard errors, that's just a different way of saying there's something wrong with the variance-covariance matrix so that's the same underlying problem, whatever it is.

Best,
Stijn

messages.subject: Re: Model with multiple mediation/moderation effects
messages.body_plain:
Well there's two problems here :-) First, whether the graphs represent the problem you're trying to solve and second, whether the graphs match the model specification.

I'll just focus on the first graph for now. To clarify, you expect:

* an effect from X on DV that may or may not be mediated by Y
* the effect of X on Y may differ depending on Z
* the moderating effect of Z may be mediated by M

If so then you're missing a X -> DV arrow to represent that the effect of X on the outcome may or may not be mediated.

When you say the moderators Z and M can affect the DV, do you mean indirectly through Y or directly as well? If the latter, then you should also have arrows from Z and M towards the Y -> DV arrow to indicate that they can moderate that relationship too.

Once we know the model you're interested in, we can have a look at the model specification.

Best,
Stijn

messages.subject: Weighted Covariance estimation using lavcor
messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan project team,
I am wondering how to compute a weighted covariance/correlation matrix using the lavcor. In the long run, I want to combine the process with missing values, but I already fail to achieve it with a full data case. The lavcor function does not have an argument for weights, but the help mentions that any arguments from lavaan can be used (in this case sampling.weights). For a minimal example of my code (with really excessive weights):

M <- matrix(c(1, 0.7, 0.7, 0.5, 0.7, 1, 0.95, 0.3, 0.7, 0.95, 1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.3, 0.3, 1),
                 nrow=4, ncol=4)
set.seed(1901)
data_small <- as.data.frame(MASS::mvrnorm(n = 30, mu = rep(0,4), Sigma = M))
weights <- c(rep(0.3, 15), rep(100000,15))
lavaan::lavCor(data_small, estimator = "ML", output = "cov", sampling.weights = weights)
lavaan::lavCor(data_small, estimator = "ML", output = "cov")

Looking at the help from the lavaan function, sampling.weights should be a variable from the dataset. Therfor, I included the weights as a variable, which would probabaly not be an option having missing values using an EM-algorithm, but it does not change anything.

data_small$weights <- weights
lavaan::lavCor(data_small, estimator = "ML", output = "cov", sampling.weights = "weights")
lavaan::lavCor(data_small[,1:4], estimator = "ML", output = "cov")

I would be glad about any pointers for corrections in the code.All the best and many thanks,
Kai

I had included that model as a more simple representation, but this might be a better representation of the effects we are predicting/interested in exploring:

We are proposing that the relationship between X and the DV is mediated by Y, but we are also interested in examining any direct effect of X on the DV. Then, with these two different paths we are hypothesizing a moderation effect in X's relationship with Y and with the DV. This moderation effect also includes a partial mediation (similarly to the X-->Y-->DV model), where Z is a direct moderator on the X-->Y link and on the X-->DV link and then also is an indirect moderator through M, so M is also a moderator of the X-->Y link and the X-->DV link, plus there is a link between Z and M. I tried to show this with the coloring, essentially that the moderation effect (Z via M) moderates the X-->Y relationship and the X-->DV relationship. Hopefully this makes sense, but I am happy to clarify further! Thank you again for your help!

messages.subject: Lots of models on a small dataset: model quality, false discovery rate
messages.subject_clean: Lots of models on a small dataset: model quality, false discovery rate
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I am unsure whether my approach is sound so I would like to ask for your help.

Background:
I am trying to fit lots of models on a small life science dataset, see the code below.
Variables p1, p2, p3, s1 and s2 denote data.frames; p4 is a numeric vector; `year` is binary.

There are several issues. As measurements are quite costly, the number of observations will be capped at around 125, but relationships are complex. Most of the data.frames cannot be efficiently reduced in dimensions (lack of multicollinearity), so fitting a "global" model on NMDS scores or PCA PCs is not satisfactory - not to mention the issues with downstream biological interpretation. So, I thought of another approach.

Instead, I am trying to assess the relationships of selected individual features from these data.frames by building models in lavaan. The number of possible models (see expand.grid below) is 368676 (!). Lots of models typically fit very well (TLI.robust, RMSEA.robust). There is also non-linearity in the data (in part due to clr transformation).

# Script:

xpg <- expand.grid(
  s1 = 1:ncol(s1),
  s2 = 1:ncol(s2),
  p1 = 1:ncol(p1),
  p2 = 1:ncol(p2),
  p3 = 1:ncol(p3)
)

initmod_raw <- c(
  'p4 ~ year',
  'p4 ~ s1',
  'p2 ~ p1',
  'p2 ~ p3',
  'p2 ~ s2',
  'p2 ~ year',
  'p2 ~ p4',
  'p1 ~ s1',
  'p1 ~ s2',
  'p1 ~ p3',
  'p1 ~ year',
  'p1 ~ p4',
  'p3 ~ s1',
  'p3 ~ s2',
  'p3 ~ year',
  'p3 ~ p4',
  's2 ~ s1')

allmod <- foreach (j = 1:nrow(xpg), .combine = "rbind") %do% {
  cur <- data.frame(
    s1 = scale(s1[, xpg[j, 1]]),
    s2 = scale(s2[, xpg[j, 2]]),
    p1 = scale(p1[, xpg[j, 3]]),
    p2 = scale(p2[, xpg[j, 4]]),
    p3 = scale(p3[, xpg[j, 5]]),
    p4 = p4, # single column variable
    year = ifelse(year == 2020, 1, 0)
  )

  lavaanmod <- paste0(initmod_raw, collapse = "\n")
  fitmod <- sem(lavaanmod, data = cur, estimator = "MLR")

  # at this point, I simplify the model iteratively by elminiating the regression with
  # the highest p.value (if p.value > 0.05) from the model, in a for loop.
  # The loop breaks if the increase in rmsea.robust.pvalue is stopped, and a final model
  # is selected. This usually results in elimination of 3-7 regressions.

  sfm <- summary(finalmod, standardized=TRUE, fit.measures=TRUE)
  sfm$fit

  # also collect weights for all models, not shown
}

quantile(allmod$chisq.scaling.factor, probs = seq(0, 1, .1))
#~        0%       10%       20%       30%       40%       50%       60%       70%
#~ 0.3844049 0.8419220 0.8801638 0.9072502 0.9307691 0.9526083 0.9750984 1.0003275
#~       80%       90%      100%
#~ 1.0322310 1.0832409 1.9845916

My questions are:
1. Literally tens of thousands of models have rmsea.robust == 0 & tli.robust >= 1. Clearly, some false discovery rate adjustment has to be used, for which my best guess currently is p.adjust(allmod$rmsea.notclose.pvalue.robust, "holm") or p.adjust(allmod$rmsea.notclose.pvalue.robust, "BH"). Would that be acceptable?

2. Several fits seem excellent, but even after iterative model simplification, there is a ratio of 1:5-7 (model parameter:observation), and there are also nonnormality issues. Is there a cutoff that can tell if the chosen models are simple enough to enable using sem() in the first place? E.g. Do I need an additional filter for models that are unreliable due to nonnormality? I was thinking of a chisq.scaling.factor filter (https://web.pdx.edu/~newsomj/semclass/ho_estimate2.pdf), but what about values smaller than 1?

Any thoughts and suggestions would be greatly appreciated.

messages.subject: Re: simsem and MG-CFA simulation
messages.body_plain:
> I'm using the package simsem on a simulation study looking at measurement invariance for ordinal data

I don't know what causes that weird issue, but my advice would be to NOT use simsem.  It is not set up for model comparison, although they wrote an anova() method that applies in the simple case of normal data.  Your code is already generating data directly from population-model syntax.  Instead of treating that as rawData= in sim() (which was only designed to generate continuous data with the same skew/kurtosis, so you will NOT get categorical data that way), you should just analyze the generated data with lavaan.  You can write a function that does the data generation, then pass that to lavaanList().  You can write another function (for the FUN= argument) to collect the output you want, including using update() to fit a more constrained invariance model.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: lavaan and censored variables
messages.body_plain:
> I would like to use this opportunity to send a warm thank to people like Yves Rosseel,  Terrence D. Jorgensen, and Ed Merkle (and many others) for their work on lavaan and associated packages. Your doing the community a great service!

Thanks for the high praise :-)

> Obviously, lavaan has been through substantial developments in recent years, but I'm not sure which limitations remain.

You can find a list of features and (tentative) plans for future developments on the home page:

https://lavaan.ugent.be/features.html

https://lavaan.ugent.be/development.html

> Is declaring factor indicators (or manifest variables in general) as censored not available in lavaan?

No, and highly doubtful.  lavaan's models all assume normality at some level (e.g., normality of latent responses underlying ordinal variables, or ML estimation of continuous data assuming normality, followed by corrections for violations thereof).  Mplus uses numerical integration to estimate models that do not rely on assuming normality (e.g., Poisson or negative-binomial distributed data).  I've seen papers implementing models for censored data in Mplus, that work by creating a binary (over the hurdle or not) and continuous (missing on the other side of the hurdle) copy of each censored variable, but that also requires numerical integration.  Numerical integration is unpardonably slow in R, so it is just not a feasible option.

Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: Weighted Covariance estimation using lavcor
messages.body_plain:
Hmm, glad you provided the reprex.  The lavCor() function estimates correlations/covariances among all the variables in object=, except the group= variable.  The sampling.weights= variable should also be excluded (and passed to lavaan() instead), but it is not.  I posted an issue on GitHub <https://github.com/yrosseel/lavaan/issues/266>.  Until it is resolved, you can set output = "fit" to get what you need:

## first obtain the parameter table for the model of interest
satFit <- lavaan::lavCor(data_small[,1:4], estimator = "ML", output = "fit")
PT <- parTable(satFit)

## then fit that model again, using sample weights
satFitW <- lavaan(PT, data_small, sampling.weights = "weights")

## without weights
lavInspect(satFit, "cov.ov")
      V1    V2    V3    V4
V1 0.887
V2 0.502 0.840
V3 0.541 0.836 0.916
V4 0.574 0.338 0.373 1.161

## accounting for weights
lavInspect(satFitW, "cov.ov")
      V1    V2    V3    V4
V1 1.039
V2 0.591 0.877
V3 0.610 0.903 1.030
V4 0.833 0.507 0.522 1.180

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: Measurement Invariance group.equal not constraining residuals
messages.subject_clean: Measurement Invariance group.equal not constraining residuals
messages.body_plain:
> the residuals are not being fixed across groups

> I also did not have success when trying to constrain the residuals "manually" in the model syntax.

You set estimator = "WLSMV" without specifying the ordered= argument, so I assume you have variables of class "ordered" in the Passed_df object (WLSMV is not appropriate for all continuous indicators).   Because you did not specify parameterization = "theta", the residual variances are not model parameters.  And you are equating intercepts, which are already equated by being fixed to zero for ordinal indicators.  They (and residual variances) can only be freed when thresholds are constrained to equality.  You can find many previous posts on this forum about categorical measurement invariance, but the semTools::measEq.syntax() function is designed to be helpful in this context (and the help-page references are enlightening).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

> why lavaan defaults to Glass's Delta instead of Cohen's D

lavaan doesn't provide either.  lavaan provides a standardized solution, in which the mean/intercept of each variable is expressed in units of that variable's SD (in that particular group or level, for multigroup or multilevel SEMs).  I only pointed out that in some situations, that parameter would be equivalent to Glass' delta.  You can calculate whatever standardized mean (difference) you are interested in.  It is not a lavaan issue.

messages.subject: Simulating Binary Exogenous Data
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am currently attempting to simulate binary exogenous data using lavaan. I’ve pared my example down to the basic concepts, but am attempting to apply these concepts to a far more complex SEM model with multiple binary predictors.

The model I’m using to simulate data is:

PopModel <- "

  X | 0*t1      !X threshold & mean at 0 for 50/50 split

  X ~ 0*1

  Y ~ .61*X    !beta coefficient

  X ~~ 1*X

  Y ~~ .6279*Y  !residual variance of Y

"

I simulated 100,000 observations to assess the accuracy of the simulated data and found that the covariance and correlation matrices in this population-level dataset are underestimating the expected effect (tested across multiple starting seeds). Below are my syntax and results.

SampData <- simulateData(PopModel,

                         sample.nobs = 100000,

                         seed = 1234)

fitted(sem(PopModel))

$cov

  Y    X

Y 1.00

X 0.61 1.00

$mean

Y X

0 0

$th

X|t1

   0

round(cov(SampData), 3)
      Y     X
Y 0.999 0.243
X 0.243 0.250

round(cor(SampData), 3)
      Y     X
Y 1.000 0.485
X 0.485 1.000

The simulated dataset shows that the binary unstandardized variance is .25, which is what I would expect for a binary variable with a 50/50 distribution (.5*.5). However, the correlation/covariance coefficients between X and Y are much lower than expected.

I’ve dug around a bit, and asked a similar question on the simsem documentation, and Terrence informed me that this is likely because the X variable is simulated at the latent response level. Since variables are standardized, simulated data in this example reflect the following interpretation: for every one SD increase in X, there is a .61 SD increase in Y. This is not what I’m wanting to obtain when simulating data with a binary exogenous variables. Instead, I’m hoping to simulate data that has the following interpretation: for every one-unit increase in X, there is a .61 SD increase in Y. This is the standard approach for interpretation of a binary variable in regression analysis.

This leads me to my question. Is there a way—using lavaan syntax (or by changing any of the population-produced matrices)—to simulate binary exogenous data in a more practical manner, where B could be interpreted as for every one-unit (not one-SD) increase in X, there is a B-SD increase in Y? Or is there a way to adjust the expected B parameter of interest in the population model, to correct for the normal-to-binary under-estimation of B that seems to happen during data generation?

I cannot seem to find another way to do this in lavaan even after closely examining current documentation, aside from using multigroup analysis, which I am hoping to avoid due to the complexity of the full model. I also know that simulating this type of data is possible with matrix notation in simsem but am hoping to use that as a last alternative if possible. Any insight moving forward would be most helpful.

Thanks,

Kaylee

messages.subject: Re: Simulating Binary Exogenous Data
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kaylee,

> I’m hoping to simulate data that has the following interpretation: for every one-unit increase in X, there is a .61 SD increase in Y. This is the standard approach for interpretation of a binary variable in regression analysis.

That is what I provided links to do in our discussion on GitHub:

https://github.com/simsem/simsem/issues/81

There is a larger tutorial associated with the second link, which explains more fully how to use the simsem-matrix approach to simulate data with binary exogenous variables.

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-022-01996-0

The context there was Monte Carlo power analysis for moderated mediation models.  But the same concepts generalize to other Monte Carlo simulations using other models with categorical exogenous variables.

>  Is there a way—using lavaan syntax

Not directly.  In this case, simsem simply passes your population model syntax to lavaan::simulateData(), which internally calculates model-implied Mu and Sigma to call MASS::mvrnorm().

If you are only simulating dummy-coded predictors, you could use multiple-group model syntax, so that the effect of X manifests as differences in endogenous-variable intercepts across groups.  The tutorial paper I linked to above also shows this approach.  However, that would get quite complicated with multiple X variables, because you have to collectively treat all the combinations of groups as arising from 1 grouping variable.

> (or by changing any of the population-produced matrices)—to simulate binary exogenous data in a more practical manner, where B could be interpreted as for every one-unit (not one-SD) increase in X, there is a B-SD increase in Y? Or is there a way to adjust the expected B parameter of interest in the population model, to correct for the normal-to-binary under-estimation of B that seems to happen during data generation?

Hmmm, maybe you could convert your group-mean difference (unstandardized effect of dummy-coded X) to the X-Y point-biserial correlation.  Than that can be converted to the biserial correlation, calculated on the assumption that X is a discrete manifestation of a latent X*.  You could specify the biserial correlation in the syntax (assuming you correctly specify Y's residual variance such that its total variance = 1), then discretize after.  Olsson's (1982) paper shows the formula linking the polyserial and point-polyserial correlations.  The biserial versions are just special cases when data are dichotomized.

https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02294164

In another tutorial, I capitalized on this transformation in a different context (maybe still relevant for your study?).  I reproduce the formula in my paper as Eq. 16, which is greatly simplified in your case because your category weights are 0 and 1, your threshold is 0, and you already know your population SD = 0.5 for a dummy code with balanced groups.  The only extra work is inverting that equation so you solve for the biserial (rho_LRV) for the given point-biserial (rho-tilde).  So once you convert your group-mean difference to a point-biserial, you multiply it by the reciprocal of the right-hand dividend in my Eq. 16 (Olsson's Eq. 11) to get the biserial you could use in syntax.

However, I think that is only a feasible solution with a single X variable.  With multiple X, you would be working with partial correlations.  This is still possible, but I expect more complicated than simply working with simsem-matrices to directly specify population effects of exogenous covariates in the metric you intend.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Jackknife for follow-up tasks
messages.body_plain:
Hi lavaan community,

I was looking for a function to perform the leave-one out Jackknife to then play with some follow up procedures (for example BCa CI). Unfortunately I didn't find anything suitable and therefore I programmed a function myself quick and dirty:

jackknife <- function(object,
                      FUN = "coef",
                      args = list(),
                      verbose = TRUE,
                      group.adjust = FALSE) {

  # Largely adopted from bootstrapLavaan
  lavmodel                  <- object@Model
  lavoptions                <- object@Options
  lavpartable               <- object@ParTable
  lavdata                   <- object@Data

  lavoptions$verbose        <- FALSE
  lavoptions$check.start    <- FALSE
  lavoptions$check.post <http://check.post>     <- FALSE
  lavoptions$optim.attempts <- 1L

  if(FUN == "coef") {
    lavoptions$baseline     <- FALSE
    lavoptions$h1           <- FALSE
    lavoptions$loglik       <- FALSE
    lavoptions$implied      <- FALSE
    lavoptions$store.vcov   <- FALSE
    lavoptions$se           <- "none"
  }

  t0 <- do.call(FUN, append(object, args))
  n  <- sum(lavTech(object, "nobs"))
  u  <- list(matrix(NA, nrow = n, ncol = length(t0)), rep(NA, times = n))
  r  <- 1

  for(g in 1 : lavdata@ngroups) {
    for(x in 1 : lavdata@nobs[[g]]) {

      if(verbose) cat("Jackknife ", round(x / n, 2) * 100, "%\r", sep = "")

      jackdata               <- lavdata
      jackdata@ov$nobs       <- lavdata@ov$nobs - 1
      jackdata@nobs[[g]]     <- lavdata@nobs[[g]] - 1
      jack...@case.idx[[g]] <- lav...@case.idx[[g]][-length(lav...@case.idx[[g]])]
      jackdata@ov$nobs       <- lavdata@ov$nobs - 1
      jackdata@norig[[g]]    <- lavdata@norig[[g]] - 1
      jackdata@X[[g]]        <- lavdata@X[[g]][-x,]
      jacksamplestats        <- try(
        lav_samplestats_from_data(
          lavdata = jackdata,
          lavoptions = lavoptions
        ), silent = TRUE
      )

      refit <- lavaan(
        slotOptions     = lavoptions,
        slotParTable    = lavpartable,
        slotModel       = lavmodel,
        slotData        = jackdata,
        slotSampleStats = jacksamplestats
      )

      u[[1]][r,] <- do.call(FUN, append(refit, args))
      u[[2]][r]  <- g

      r <- r + 1

    }
  }

  if(group.adjust) {
    for(g in 1 : lavdata@ngroups) {
      for(c in 1 : ncol(u[[1]])) {
        rc <- unique(round(u[[1]][u[[2]] == g, c], 4))
        if(length(rc) == 1) u[[1]][u[[2]] == g, c] <- NA
      }
    }
  }

  u <- u[[1]]

  coef <- sapply(rep(1 : ncol(u)), function(x, u, t0) {
    t0 <- t0[x]
    u  <- na.omit(u[, x])
    n  <- length(u)
    c(
      bias = (mean(u) - t0) * (n - 1),
      se = sqrt(((n - 1) / n) * sum((u - mean(u))^2))
    )
  }, u, t0)

  try(colnames(u) <- names(t0), silent = TRUE)

  out <- list(
    t0   = t0,
    u    = u,
    bias = coef[1,],
    se   = coef[2,]
  )

  class(out) <- "jackknife"
  out

}

summary.jackknife <- function(object, dec = 3) {
  round(
    cbind(
      t0   = object$t0,
      bias = object$bias,
      se   = object$se
    ),
    dec
  )
}

# Example
HS.model <- '
visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
'

fit <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, meanstructure = TRUE)
jk  <- jackknife(fit)
summary(jk)

This is just a prototype. Warning: The coefs may even be miscalculated.

I have 2 basic questions. If anyone wants to give me input, I would be very grateful:

(1) For the Jackknife, I need to update the lavaan data slot to do the resampling. I can find the utility function lav_data_update, but the documentation says "A list of (new) data matrices (per group) of the same size". This does not fit to the Jackknife. Is there another internal utility function for the problem? If not, is my solution (highlighted in yellow) sufficient or is this not a good idea?

(2) For multi-group models the procedure seems dubious to me (leave-one out). If a data set in one group is omitted, it obviously has no effect on the coefficients of the other group. "se" and "bias" seem to be biased by this. I did include a "solution" (highlighted in red). But this is naive and anything but good. Any ideas or references? I can't find anything related to this case.

Best

Christian

Hi Christian,

How about this? In your call to lavaan() using slots, do not use `slotData` and `slotSampleStats`, and use the argument `data` directly. As far as I understand, if these slots are not supplied, then `data` (or other arguments like `sample.cov` and `sample.nobs`) will be used. lavInspect() can be used to retrieve the data used, with column names included.

Maybe you have already tried this and this did not work? if it didn't, I would like to know.

There may be a more efficient solution. Anyway, my two cents.

By the way, BCa is already available, though only for single group for now (https://lavaan.ugent.be/history/dot6.html). (Not yet mentioned in the help page, it seems.)

-- Shu Fai

messages.subject: RE: Jackknife for follow-up tasks
messages.body_plain:
Hi Shu Fai,

thanks for your advice. To do this, you would need to supply the jackknife function with the data as an additional argument or generate a data.frame from the data slot. The former is very messy. I have also written a function for the latter. However, that seems to me to be the worse and more error-prone option.

Best

Christian

Von: lav...@googlegroups.com <lav...@googlegroups.com> im Auftrag von Shu Fai Cheung (張樹輝) <shufai...@gmail.com>
Gesendet: Sonntag, 26. Februar 2023 15:16
An: lavaan <lav...@googlegroups.com>
Betreff: Re: Jackknife for follow-up tasks

Hi Christian,

How about this? In your call to lavaan() using slots, do not use `slotData` and `slotSampleStats`, and use the argument `data` directly. As far as I understand, if these slots are not supplied, then `data` (or other arguments like `sample.cov` and `sample.nobs`) will be used. lavInspect() can be used to retrieve the data used, with column names included.

Maybe you have already tried this and this did not work? if it didn't, I would like to know.

There may be a more efficient solution. Anyway, my two cents.

By the way, BCa is already available, though only for single group for now (https://lavaan.ugent.be/history/dot6.html). (Not yet mentioned in the help page, it seems.)

-- Shu Fai

On Sunday, February 26, 2023 at 9:20:53 PM UTC+8 christia...@hhl.de wrote:
> Hi lavaan community,
>
> I was looking for a function to perform the leave-one out Jackknife to then play with some follow up procedures (for example BCa CI). Unfortunately I didn't find anything suitable and therefore I programmed a function myself quick and dirty:
>
> jackknife <- function(object,
>                       FUN = "coef",
>                       args = list(),
>                       verbose = TRUE,
>                       group.adjust = FALSE) {
>
>
>   # Largely adopted from bootstrapLavaan
>   lavmodel                  <- object@Model
>   lavoptions                <- object@Options
>   lavpartable               <- object@ParTable
>   lavdata                   <- object@Data
>
>   lavoptions$verbose        <- FALSE
>   lavoptions$check.start    <- FALSE
>   lavoptions$check.post <http://check.post>     <- FALSE
>   lavoptions$optim.attempts <- 1L
>
>   if(FUN == "coef") {
>     lavoptions$baseline     <- FALSE
>     lavoptions$h1           <- FALSE
>     lavoptions$loglik       <- FALSE
>     lavoptions$implied      <- FALSE
>     lavoptions$store.vcov   <- FALSE
>     lavoptions$se           <- "none"
>   }
>
>   t0 <- do.call(FUN, append(object, args))
>   n  <- sum(lavTech(object, "nobs"))
>   u  <- list(matrix(NA, nrow = n, ncol = length(t0)), rep(NA, times = n))
>   r  <- 1
>
>   for(g in 1 : lavdata@ngroups) {
>     for(x in 1 : lavdata@nobs[[g]]) {
>
>       if(verbose) cat("Jackknife ", round(x / n, 2) * 100, "%\r", sep = "")
>
>       jackdata               <- lavdata
>       jackdata@ov$nobs       <- lavdata@ov$nobs - 1
>       jackdata@nobs[[g]]     <- lavdata@nobs[[g]] - 1
>       jack...@case.idx[[g]] <- lav...@case.idx[[g]][-length(lav...@case.idx[[g]])]
>       jackdata@ov$nobs       <- lavdata@ov$nobs - 1
>       jackdata@norig[[g]]    <- lavdata@norig[[g]] - 1
>       jackdata@X[[g]]        <- lavdata@X[[g]][-x,]
>       jacksamplestats        <- try(
>         lav_samplestats_from_data(
>           lavdata = jackdata,
>           lavoptions = lavoptions
>         ), silent = TRUE
>       )
>
>       refit <- lavaan(
>         slotOptions     = lavoptions,
>         slotParTable    = lavpartable,
>         slotModel       = lavmodel,
>         slotData        = jackdata,
>         slotSampleStats = jacksamplestats
>       )
>
>       u[[1]][r,] <- do.call(FUN, append(refit, args))
>       u[[2]][r]  <- g
>
>       r <- r + 1
>
>     }
>   }
>
>
>   if(group.adjust) {
>     for(g in 1 : lavdata@ngroups) {
>       for(c in 1 : ncol(u[[1]])) {
>         rc <- unique(round(u[[1]][u[[2]] == g, c], 4))
>         if(length(rc) == 1) u[[1]][u[[2]] == g, c] <- NA
>       }
>     }
>   }
>
>   u <- u[[1]]
>
>   coef <- sapply(rep(1 : ncol(u)), function(x, u, t0) {
>     t0 <- t0[x]
>     u  <- na.omit(u[, x])
>     n  <- length(u)
>     c(
>       bias = (mean(u) - t0) * (n - 1),
>       se = sqrt(((n - 1) / n) * sum((u - mean(u))^2))
>     )
>   }, u, t0)
>
>   try(colnames(u) <- names(t0), silent = TRUE)
>
>   out <- list(
>     t0   = t0,
>     u    = u,
>     bias = coef[1,],
>     se   = coef[2,]
>   )
>
>   class(out) <- "jackknife"
>   out
>
> }
>
> summary.jackknife <- function(object, dec = 3) {
>   round(
>     cbind(
>       t0   = object$t0,
>       bias = object$bias,
>       se   = object$se
>     ),
>     dec
>   )
> }
>
>
> # Example
> HS.model <- '
> visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
> textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
> speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
> '
>
> fit <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, meanstructure = TRUE)
> jk  <- jackknife(fit)
> summary(jk)
>
>
> This is just a prototype. Warning: The coefs may even be miscalculated.
>
> I have 2 basic questions. If anyone wants to give me input, I would be very grateful:
>
> (1) For the Jackknife, I need to update the lavaan data slot to do the resampling. I can find the utility function lav_data_update, but the documentation says "A list of (new) data matrices (per group) of the same size". This does not fit to the Jackknife. Is there another internal utility function for the problem? If not, is my solution (highlighted in yellow) sufficient or is this not a good idea?
>
> (2) For multi-group models the procedure seems dubious to me (leave-one out). If a data set in one group is omitted, it obviously has no effect on the coefficients of the other group. "se" and "bias" seem to be biased by this. I did include a "solution" (highlighted in red). But this is naive and anything but good. Any ideas or references? I can't find anything related to this case.
>
> Best
>
> Christian

--

model1 = 'LV1=~a1+a2+a3

LV4=~d1+d2+d3
LV5=~e1+e2+e3
LV6=~f1+f2+f3

LV3 ~ c(a1, a2)*LV1 + c(a3, a4)*LV2
LV4~LV3+LV1+LV2

LV6~LV5+LV4+LV3+LV1+LV2

diffLV1 := a1 - a2
diffLV2 := a3 - a4  '

modelfit1 = sem(model1, data = data, group = "group", ordered = TRUE)
summary(modelfit1, standardized=T, fit.measures=T)

1. I was wondering if the comparison is done within constrained model or this comparison is done in SEM base / configural model ?

Thanks
Saeed

On Tue, 11 Oct 2022 at 16:00, 'Keith Markus' via lavaan <lav...@googlegroups.com> wrote:

> Saeed,
> I believe you have already been through levels of invariance and have focused on the appropriate level for mean comparisons.  The next thing to consider is how many items the scales have.  If you have more than a few items in each scale, it may be worth investigating partial invariance, which means that invariance holds for a subset of items but not all of them.  If you can find an invariant subset of items, you may be able to use those for mean comparisons across groups.  If not, then you can report the descriptive results with the explanation that you cannot distinguish group differences in means from group differences in how they respond to the scales.  You can report the measurement invariance analysis and offer a word of caution for other researchers using the same measure to compare mean differences.
>

messages.subject: Re: CFA
messages.body_plain:
Thank you Jermy!  The syntax used for our model ( just identifird) is the following :
cfamodel<- "ABC=~ a1 + a2 + 1*a3"
sdata[,c("a1",   "a2",   "a3")] <-lapply(data[,c(  ("a1",   "a2",  "a3")], ordered)

CFA model: fit<-cfa(cfamodel, data=sdata,std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

Configural: model1 <- cfa(cfamodel, data = sdata, group = "Gender", std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE)
Metric: model2 <- cfa(cfamodel, data = sdata, group = "Gender", std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE,group.equal = c("loadings"))
scalar :model31 <- cfa(cfamodel, data = sdata, group = "Gender", std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE, group.equal = c("loadings","thresholds"))

Can you tell me is that the right practice?
Grace

messages.subject: Re: Latent Variable with Two Indicators
messages.body_plain:
Hi Everyone,
I was wondering how I would specify a latent variable with only two indicators in a longitudinal research design. The construct is measured at both time points. Do I constrain both indicators to one and the intercept of both indicatorsto to zero?

Thanks in advance for any help or advice!

Lukas

Terrence Jorgensen schrieb am Montag, 12. Februar 2018 um 16:31:44 UTC+1:
> > I should constrain the loadings to be equal, and then constrain the higher order Latent variance to 1?
>
> Or constrain both loadings to be 1, and estimate the factor variance (which will simply be the covariance between the two indicators, clearly illustrating why a second-order factor model with only 2 indicators adds no information beyond a first-order factor model).
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
